What do you think, executor?

Their words are full of passion and questioning, unlike the short, cold orders you're familiar with.
You don't want to disappoint these nice big hats.
You think carefully about what they said and start to understand their point.
The crab-faced lord nods, but the big hats seem less pleased. Did you say something wrong?

Bewildered, you simply wait quietly for the next order. As you've learned from Manus Vindictae, lords and ladies are often very busy. You must be patient.
Your expression seems to cheer them up again.
You're confused, but you're glad to see them happy.
You don't really understand what they mean, so you repeat a few words you remember.
ㄌㄚㄕ-Rationality ... ㄉ-death?
A purely thoughtless answer! The perfect executor indeed!
A veritable prophet!
They all take turns praising you, and while you're not sure why, you feel happy too.
She has broken free from the limits of thought! She understands neither words nor logic! A perfect executor!

Brushing aside these confusing matters, your mind turns to food instead. In the blue room, your comrades would bring you a meal right about now.
But here, no one notices your rumbling belly, so you speak up.

Some big hats immediately bring you food. It may be late, but it tastes much better than what your comrades used to give you.
This place is nice. Perhaps you'll stay a few more days to enjoy the meals.

You enter a dim cave where the walls are painted with dancing skeletons.
The big hats stop and, copying the skeletons' movements, begin to dance.
The "Danse Macabre." I should have known ... Headless ones, what's this all about?
May I remind you that we must perform the ritual? Time cannot be wasted.
The big hats ignore his question and keep on dancing. The crab-faced lord sighs and looks at you.
You're their "chosen one," Coppélia. Do something.
Excellent question!

Death is a rejection of our capitalist, utilitarian society. It is an act of pure self-determination—a breaking free from material constraints. You might say that the pursuit of death is life's greatest journey ...
Death is ㄍ-good?
Oh no, death is the worst thing in the world! Which is precisely why those who seek it truly possess free will!

"Do something" is a vague order, so you decide to join the big hats. The crab-faced lord doesn't stop you.
Oh! You're certain this was the right choice.
You take two more steps to the middle of the big hats and move your legs to the beat.
Bravo! Dance with us unto death!
They're pleased with your movements. As your shadows dance wildly in the cave, the crab-faced lord stands silent, waiting for you to finish. It seems you've followed orders perfectly.
The painted skeletons catch your attention, their strange dance seemingly pushing you away. You can't bring yourself to get any closer to the wall or the big hats.
They notice your reaction and stop dancing to cover your eyes.
Get out! Get out! Our executor cannot fear death! It would ruin her!
You leave the cave in complete darkness. The crab-faced lord seems pleased that you've learned how to handle the big hats.

Your arm seems to be some sort of tool or instrument ... but it makes no sound.
Does it serve a purpose?
Noticing the light reflected off your arm from the streetlight, the big hats gather around it like moths to a flame.
You try to make your arm move the way the orchestra taught you.
A lovely melody plays from your arm. The big hats nod, speaking your praises.
Have you understood something?
Not at all, but I feel like nodding.
Very good. Best not forget you're one of the Headless!
You seem to have missed a step. Your arm swings aimlessly in the air, making no sound but the whistling of the wind.
You wait quietly for what the others will say.
Hmm ... then this arm is just like any other.

Yes, your arm has nothing special besides its appearance.
How utterly wonderful! How useless and incapable!
Here, take this mille-feuille. And be sure to keep your arm just as it is.
That's not fighting. You're just waving it around like a monkey with a stick.
If you wish to serve the Guiding One, you must better your skills.

Hmm ... hmm ... like a monkey with a stick. I'd say that's rather good, wouldn't you?
You can fight, hunt, gobble down your enemies—revel in all the simple, carefree joys of an animalistic life!
ㄧ-Eat?! No!

As you wander through the city, unsure of which direction to take, a strange, powerful vibration hits you.
After a while you track down the source. It's a ladder suspended in midair. Two people stand nearby, one of them about to climb.
As you stare at this unusual ladder, melodies both familiar and unfamiliar play in your mind. Where could a floating ladder possibly lead?

The melodies surrounding the ladder feel unsettled and dangerous. Falling would hurt.
You try to warn them, but as the words leave your lips, the climber falls. The melodies fade, and the ladder disappears.
The person standing back silently watches you. You notice that his note feels like that of the lords.
You just ruined a precious chance for experimentation ... Go think about what you've done. I don't want you coming near me again.

They always tell you to leave. He must be a lord you haven't met before.
You obey and leave quickly.

Not fully understanding what's happening, you decide to stay and observe.
Then, something strange happens. The climber disappears into the melodies, and the other begins writing and muttering something.
That's all.
You and the big hats come across another crowd, the same people you met earlier, but now they're chanting even louder.

A bunch of fools. Aware of their shackles but unable to break free from them.
They're trapped in this sad world but haven't figured out how to escape it, so they're turning back into beasts ...
Hm? Is there something you want to say?
You carefully explain that some of these people are your friends.
Friends? I see, I see—then let's study their animalistic nature.
It is the second easiest way to attain freedom. A little rough, but very effective!

You hear mentions of "liberty" and "breaking free" from among the crowd, and it makes you wonder. Why do they care so much about these things?
Suddenly, you feel you have a lot of questions to ask.

With the crab-faced lord standing nearby, you instinctively feel you should think carefully about what you say.
You decide to ask the thing you most want to know.
They don't like order. Why?

You receive a variety of answers.
The crowd says order prevents them from truly living. The big hats say this is part of the fight against the universe.
The crab-faced lord says, "What kind of question is that? Enough talk. Let's get to work."

You struggle to come up with the right question. In the end, nothing comes out.
Feeling anxious, you fall back to your old way of speaking and roar, garnering another round of cheers from the big hats, but still no answers.
To create a perfect dissonant symphony often requires purging a few noises to reach true cacophony.

You find the source of the metallic sound. It looks like a "tuning fork." Before you can examine it, it lets out a sharp shriek and darts toward a door.
The door slowly opens for you—perhaps more fascinating sounds await inside.

You find the source of the metallic sound behind the blocks. It's a delicate little "tuning fork." 
You tap it, and its ripples echo around you. The rainbow-colored door behind you opens, and from within come even more fascinating sounds, awaiting your reception.

You hear the cotton candy sing a syrupy tune. You reshape it into a "tuning fork," and when you look again, it has turned into a real "tuning fork."
You fit it into the keyhole of the door behind you. The door opens, and more delightful sounds await inside.

You try to quietly get away from the roaring and hide behind the treasure chest. Only to accidentally step on something metallic.
You pick it up—it's a delicate little tuning fork.

You move closer to the source of the roar. Despite the noise, you hear another faint sound trying to resonate with you.
You approach—revealing a delicate "tuning fork," hiding alone in the corner.

With a click, the door leaking blueberry jam ripples open. A wave of sound engulfs you.
You walk toward its source.

You push the door open, and strands of silver brush against your nose, fingers, and hair.
You blink and see that they're notes flowing like a stream, weaving around a music disc.

You push the door open and see rows of ragdoll heads grinning and flipping through the air, their stitched mouths chanting a familiar tune.
"Oh hey! Oh hey! Look at this wheat stalk! Oh hey! Let's see who, who, who'll be eaten!"

You push the door open and step inside. A crowd of striped pajama-clad figures dances around a boiling cauldron.
Inside the pot, several Critters leap and twist to the rhythm. You find their tempo and join the melody yourself.

You push the door open and see notes falling onto the rotted harp vines of a great tree.
You touch one note. It bounces away and lands on a drumhead covered in mushrooms.

You push the door open, but it suddenly turns into a fence. As you stumble through, a black-robed person appears before you.
He grabs your single-string arm, yanks it upward, and throws it aside.

You find the source of the metallic sound. It looks like a "tuning fork." Before you can examine it, it lets out a sharp shriek and darts toward a door.
You stare at the door until it finally speaks: "What are you still waiting for?"

You find the source of the metallic sound behind the blocks. It's a delicate little "tuning fork."
You tap it, watching the ripples slowly spread, but you can't make sense of the strange melody. It seems uninterested in communicating with you.

You hear the cotton candy sing a syrupy tune. You reshape the soft candy into a "tuning fork."
You give it a taste—it tastes like licking metal. You give up immediately.

You make the logical choice to avoid the source of the roar, but as you do, you step on a piece of metal. Suddenly the roaring stops.
Your slumbering comrade jolts awake, grabs you by your arm, and hurls you away.

You move closer to the source of the roar. Despite the noise, you hear another faint sound trying to resonate with you.
You approach—revealing a delicate "tuning fork," hiding alone in the corner.
Want to sing with me?
Your innocence is purer than gold itself, giving life a weight beyond value.
You're unsure what this odd bird eats, but after picking through your offerings, she happily swallows a coin whole and begins to sing with renewed gusto.
You open the cage, and she flies out, but her wingbeats waver with uncertainty. She seems unsure where to go, eventually settling in your palm.

You can't manage the lock. After repeated failures, frustration sets in.
Perhaps to comfort you, the little bird gifts you a feather.

You approach the owner, hand over a few Goldfinch Coins, and open one barrel.
The rich, nutty aroma wrapped in milky sweetness reminds you of the lady with honeyed scents.
So this is what a devil tastes like.

You open the barrel before you. The rich aroma wrapped in milky sweetness reminds you of the lady with honeyed scents.
So this is what a devil tastes like.

You once again find the owner, hand over a few Goldfinch Coins, and open another barrel.
This time, a gentle powdery sweetness and floral fragrance embrace you. Turns out devils come in different flavors.

You approach the owner, hand over a few Goldfinch Coins, and open that barrel.
This time, a gentle powdery sweetness and floral fragrance embrace you. Turns out devils come in different flavors.
You open another barrel. The gentle powdery sweetness and floral fragrance embrace you. Turns out devils come in different flavors.

For the third flavor of the devil, you once again find the owner and open the third barrel.
This time, the devil tastes like peach.
You open another barrel and share the peach-flavored devil with the children.

The sound of opening the barrel draws the owner's attention.
A hard swat from his walking stick sends you and the chirping children flying away.

For the third flavor of the devil, you find the owner, hand over some Goldfinch Coins, and open the third barrel.
This time, the devil tastes like peach.

The children grow more excited, crowding around you once again by another barrel.
Perhaps this devil has a unique flavor too.

No one seems to wonder if these devils have a fourth flavor, except you.
Dizzy from downing three barrels of "Diabolo," you notice one last barrel in the corner. Its lid is half open, easy to drink from directly, yet none of the children approach it.

The children, having tasted one barrel, now crave another.
They crowd around you by the next one.

The barrel holding the fourth devil starts to move on its own. You're startled but leap onto it and pry it open. Only to find, not a drink, but a complicated machine inside. Though it could be just a hallucination from the other devil's brews.

The barrel holding the fourth devil starts to move on its own. You're startled but lunge toward it, toppling it over.
In a daze, you see an angry figure appear—perhaps the devil within seeking his revenge, or maybe just the furious owner.
The honey-scented lady warned you not to indulge too much in sweetness, so you decide to leave the noisy children behind.
Your stomach can't handle another devil. You decide to leave the noisy children behind.

You're not sure what to say, but "It's good" always seems to please people.
Sure enough, he leaps with joy.

No one's ever asked you such a question before. You tilt your head, lost in thought.
He watches you with growing interest before excitedly declaring that his art must have totally captivated you.
Disappointed, he hurls his brush aside, tears the painting off, and hands it to you.
Your stuttering praise seems to work anyway. He resumes splashing paint onto the canvas with renewed energy.

No one's ever asked you such a question before. You tilt your head, lost in confusion.
In your silence, he stares at the canvas, starts painting again, and soon forgets you. You take the chance to slip away.

You tap your left hand lightly, and a short melody bounces between the layers of paint.
You describe what you feel honestly. The colors seem a bit disordered.
He takes your tapping as mockery, and it lights his temper.

You tap your left hand lightly, and a short melody bounces between the layers of paint.
You describe what you feel honestly. The colors seem a bit chaotic.
Throw this away for me. Anywhere will do. Just away.

The merchant buried under a mountain of merchandise offers a discount. Turns out the item wasn't worth his first price. 
You seem to have learned a thing or two about trade.

The Goldfinch Coins chirp, begging not to be handed over, yet the sale is so tempting.
The shopkeeper, lost behind his mountains of goods, can't see your movements. You turn and run.
The merchant buried under a mountain of merchandise grows impatient and starts recommending other items.

The Goldfinch Coins chirp, begging you not to hand them over, yet the sale is so tempting.
But the shopkeeper, buried in his goods, notices your intent and kicks you out.
You've got a good eye. This is one of our very best items!
You crouch down and tap the pocket watch, trying to find its sound.
You twist the crown, and the hands begin to move with the gears. It seems they're not as weary as you thought.

You see the second hand follow the minute hand, and the minute hand follow the hour hand. The monotone rhythm against your fingertips resonates with your strings.
Then you notice a fourth hand. You realize this might be the harmony you've been seeking.
You sing in duet with the musical watch until a crowd surges past from the street outside. Among them, one man steps out and approaches you.
As you move the still fourth hand, the watch opens its heart. Its "soundboard" rises, and the "wheel" and "tone bars" play a waltz.
The echo you expected doesn't ripple back. Only a faint vibration stirs around you without spreading further.
You see the hands hesitate, lifeless and limp. You quickly lose patience.

You see the second hand follow the minute hand, and the minute hand follow the hour hand. The monotone rhythm against your fingertips resonates with your strings.
But before you can react, the hands all stop at once, becoming lifeless and inert.
As you move the still fourth hand, the watch opens its heart. The "soundboard" cracks, the "wheel" flies off, and the "tone bars" fall apart. The music notes at last stop dancing in the air.
I heard ... your sounds ... But why no echoes? You ... don't like it?
I don't like talking to people who don't answer me either.
The bell chimes! France bleeds! There's no time to waste, but I no longer know the time! Demoiselle, I need your watch.
So that's how you speak. It's not pretty, nor fun, nor at all familiar ... but I'm glad to hear you again all the same.
You crawl into a strange tent following the voice and find some dusty instruments. Most are cracked and old, but a few can still be played.
You don't know where to go. But the worn tent looks cozy, so you crawl inside and fall fast asleep.
You follow the voice, digging through the muddy ground, but only find bubbles rising from the muck. You poke them and find some joy in the rhythm of the popping foam.

You crawl into a strange tent following the voice and uncover a chipped wooden box. Opening it, you hear a familiar tune.
You hum along: "First dance, all went well; second dance, slipped and fell; third dance, bridge collapsed ..."
You gaze into the white crystal, where a reflection of you crying appears. You don't remember ever crying so hard.
The green crystal fills your whole body with warmth. You like the feeling. It fills you with strength.
The crystals on the cabinet tremble slightly, and from their resonance, you catch a faint melody.
The golden gleam draws your attention. You see yourself stuffing coins into your pockets—but you can't recall when that happened.
Forgetting the absent shopkeeper, your presence surprises the sprites. You dance with them until they're exhausted, though you feel oddly invigorated.

The note says:
"Nowadays, no one knows where life's paths will take them. There's no need to doubt or worry, as no one expects you to make a decision right away. Sometimes, even the line between good and evil disappears."

You mimic the others and toss in your coin.
The water ripples and swirls; perhaps that surge of sound is the result of the ritual.

You try to scoop up a handful of water to uncover the ritual's secret. After several attempts, you confirm that all the fountain contains is ordinary water—but you've picked up quite a few coins as well.

You mimic the others and toss in your coin.
Nothing happens. All that changes is the crisp sound of the Goldfinch Coin as it hits the water.

You mimic the others and toss in your coin.
The fountain erupts in a massive surge of water, splashing you from head to toe. The roar of the waves answers you.

Some open wooden crates are being carried further into the banquet hall. You catch the scent of fresh plant shoots, animal blood, and strange spices. Your stomach feels empty, and a strange vibration runs through you.
A crab-faced lord in a suit is watching the workers. He notices you and waves a claw.
Just arrived, have you? I don't believe I've seen you before. Invited by Laurent Roseau as well?
ㄚ ... I am Coppélia.
Noted. I'll verify your details later. You may call me Taira.
No need to be stiff. I just arrived in Paris myself. These people simply lack discipline—someone must keep them in order.
Work piles on us in mountains, yet those who claim to follow the Guiding One remain languid. Tsk.
You have work to do too. Direct them to move the boxes, just as Lyra directs you.
You and your comrades silently sync up. They place their crates down and sing in a beautiful chorus.
... I told you to direct the moving, not sing.
I will handle this. Just stay out of the way.
Your instructions lead to chaos. Boxes fall, supplies spill, and the crab-faced lord scratches his head with a claw.
Even a simple task proved too much, hm?
Go bother Hypothetik or Lyra. I will handle this.

A little lady in formal wear sits on a tall chair, looking exactly as she did years ago.
She gazes out of the window, and although her face is hidden, you can tell she's intently listening to "the whispers of the wind."
When she hears your footsteps, she turns toward you.
It's been some time, Coppélia. How have you been? Taking care of your arm, I hope?
She looks directly at your arm, just like she always does, paying more attention to it than to you. You remember the days when she picked out instruments for you.
I hear you reached the banquet hall all on your own. Quite impressive.
But tell me—why are you in Paris? Who brought you here?
ㄋ-Nectar ...

Nectar ... ah, her, was it? Or perhaps ...? Why is it you can't remember names?
Do you remember my name?
ㄌ-ㄌㄚ, er, Lie ...
*chuckle* It's Lyra. Remember that—not "Liar" or "Lawyer," alright?
She smiles at you but doesn't say anything more. The air seems to grow cool, urging you to leave.

In the dimly lit hall, you notice a lady glowing with flames, casting a blue light across the room.
She's standing across from a masked comrade dripping thick slime. A sickle-shaped shadow stretches from the comrade to her hand.

The comrade whimpers weakly.
Whether this is a scolding or a punishment, you'd rather not be involved. Still, you hear their words.

I hear you. Your pain comes from doubt in your choices.
This is not uncommon.
But a word of caution: Those who waver during the mask trial are not favored by the Guiding One. You'd best think on that before you act.

The thick black slime shimmers with light as the lady gestures for you to approach.
When you get closer, you feel no heat from her flames.
This one is unsettled. He hesitates to wear the mask.

Your arrival is timely. His pain is real but brief. Soon, he will forget it and become an instrument ...
You, too, play to our music—consider this an early introduction.
The workers' anger seems to have clear boundaries, and they show a surprising amount of patience with your confusion now they're not protesting.

You hear a mix of voices talking about low pay, hungry children, and feeling exhausted all the time.
Some of their stories sound oddly familiar, even though you've never seen a factory or received any "wages." You listen like you're hearing a bedtime story.
I get hungry too ... ㄨㄟ-Wages? Buying? ... ㄚ?

You watch them all put on a face, as though they're proud of their anger. They ask you to stand up straight, stretch your arms, and shout their slogans. You do it a few times, and they cheer.
They seem to think you're feeling something called "dignity," but you're just waving your arms around, getting nothing from these chaotic vibrations.

You notice someone with an armband weaving through the crowd, asking people questions.
They sound familiar with each other, but a mix of anger and frustration simmers just beneath the surface.
You find out he's one of the protest leaders, a workers' representative who is thoughtful and deserves respect. People praise him, but you also hear some arguments.
I don't understand why he believes in these Beasts—no one's ever even seen the things!
There's no proof linking the disappearances to any sort of beast at all. Has anyone actually heard a howl or found a single claw mark?
So, he's telling us to be on the lookout for something nobody has ever seen. Pft. We aren't scared of that! We aren't scared of anything!
The city's melody starts to shake, pulling the crowd into its rhythm. You see them getting more excited. No amount of shouting seems to tire them.

They tell you to "go home before dark" and "stay indoors when you can," trying to scare you with stories of recent disappearances. Meanwhile, the man with the armband asks if anyone has seen the Beasts of Gévaudan.
Listen, if we start believing in these Beasts, it'll just mean we've fallen into their trap! They're using this rumor to stop our protest—just look at our representative! He's already bought into it!
Right! It's true people have been disappearing, but that is exactly why we need to stick together! No Beasts will break our line or our resolve!
This brightly colored animal used to be part of the crowd, but now it only roars. Its friends don't seem surprised by this, as if it were always this way.
*roar*
Using your usual way of communicating with your comrades, you figure out what it wants.
It enjoys its new form and feels powerful in its return to beasthood. It no longer worries about work or time; it can now devote its entire life to merely living.

You both wave your bodies and roar for a while. Then, it returns to the group, raises its clawed arm, and barks loudly. You raise your left arm too, letting the wind whistle through it. You're not sure why—or what the beast means by it.
Welcome to Magazine de Georges, little one. How may I help you today?

We are the Headless. The Headless Georges, if you will. We wear hats when we're out and about to avoid scaring anyone.
But enough about us, who are you?
They all wear big hats that cover their entire heads, but the hats don't seem hollow. Perhaps there's a drum hidden underneath.​
ㄚ-I am Coppélia.
Ah, an elegant name—reminds me of a ballet. Perhaps that's why your parents chose it.
ㄚ-I don't ㄋ-know.
From the original book, then. Whichever was to your parent's liking.
ㄚ-I don't know who my parents are.
Oh, my apologies ... I meant the people who raised you.
There were many, but they never spoke, never watched ㄅㄚˊㄌㄟˋ-ballets ... didn't give names either, I don't think.
I'm sorry, do you mean to say you were raised by people who couldn't speak?
ㄧ-Yes, they never spoke. I learned to speak from the lords and ladies. They ㄎㄚˋ-called me Coppélia.
Everyone! I believe I've found the perfect candidate for the ritual!

As I mentioned, this is Magazine de Georges, where we print our thoughts into booklets for all the city to read.
Tell me, where do you come from?
ㄚ-I can't tell you.
Haha, keeping secrets, I see. You must come from somewhere very special indeed—which explains why you caught my eye.
ㄚ-I don't understand. What's "ㄙㄅㄟ-special"? My room is just ... blue.
Plain can be good too. It saves energy—allows one to focus on what's outside.
I don't go ㄠˋㄘㄞˋ-outside much. This is ... my first time? Second? ... ㄙㄜˋ-Third?
Hmm ... so you've mostly lived in an empty room, and you can count your forays to the great outdoors on one hand.
ㄧ-Yes.
Why isn't the executor here? This is bad.
No, it's not your fault. It's just that we were to meet the executor soon. I'm hoping he's running late.
ㄅ-But ... being on time is good, right?

Not at all! People who focus too much on time work far too hard and act far too human.
People like you, who take no notice of the passage of time, are far superior.
... Wait, I've got an idea! Come, sit down. Can I offer you tea? Coffee?

We borrowed one from a secret organization.
He lacks initiative, disregards society, and all-round has the mind of an animal—a perfect fit for the ritual.
Unfortunately, he loves to work. Never tires of it, in fact, and is always punctual.
*tut* ... What we really need is someone who's no good at working. Someone who can't work at all, even—perhaps as the result of some malady or other.
Your left arm ... was it always like that?
ㄚ... I don't remember.
... I see. Come, sit. Could I offer you a tea? Coffee?

Land floats in the sky, beasts peacefully tear at each other, and the big hats vent their emotions—all while the crab-faced lord concentrates on preparing the ritual site.
You watch quietly until everything is ready. Then someone pushes you into the middle of the crowd.
It is time. Are you ready?
You follow the order without question. After all, it is just another among many—another action imposed upon your empty life.
Then begin the ritual—cut off our heads! Let us fight like living beings, while you free us from the slavery of mental anguish so that we may truly live!
What did you say?
Don't ㄨ-want to kill people ... ㄋ-Not good.

This is only a ritual. It will not truly kill them. Their lives will be restored afterward ...
*sigh* It's difficult to explain. Just know this: they chose this. You need only obey.
But ... ㄎㄚ-cutting heads hurts. Big hats will hurt. Death is ... scary and ㄉㄧˋㄙ-disgusting ...

*sigh* Friendship and conscience, the lowest form of logic and thought. It seems our executor cannot do her duty.
The deal is off, Taira. What a shame.
If she cannot do it, I will. Our agreement will proceed without issue.

Cutting heads must be painful, and people without heads can't even scream.
This city has taught you that silence and pain are never good, so you block the crab-faced lord's path.
ㄋ-No! My comrades are nice ... but city people are ㄈ-fun! Big hats are ㄍ-good! You leave them alone!
Instinct compels you to put a stop to it all.
Bubbles form at the crab's mouth, like the foam your comrades from the sea make. The crab-faced lord sighs and points the blade at you.

... I am not your gentle guardian. If you intend to behave like a child, step aside.
If you hinder the mission, I will show you no mercy.

The subtle fragrance of nectar works its way into your dream and wakes you from your sleep.
Even with your eyes shut, you can tell this isn't the room you usually stay in.
Still, no matter where you look, the space is colored Klein Blue—just like everywhere else.

You try to sink back into the comfort of darkness, but the sweet scent stimulates your senses.
In the end, you're forced awake in a room drenched in Klein Blue.

You roll and turn as you stretch off the stiffness of a long rest, exploring the space as you do so.
It feels meaninglessly empty. You could roll around a few more times without hitting a thing.

You notice some notes prominently displayed on the wall. The closest has words that even you can read:
What you need is on the next note. Or you could just lie back down. It's safe here for now.
"What you need" ... You think about it, but your mind comes up blank. But you know what the words are asking.

A city you've never seen before comes into view. Its lights chase away the darkness, and its melody rings out loud and free.
You can sense where your comrades are. Their voices lurk beneath the city's own beat, faint, almost imperceptible, just like you and your left arm.
Your guardian has found you a city where you can go wherever you please.
What you really need is a safe place to stay. Sticking close to your comrades might be the best way to do that right now. Everything else can wait.

Strange feelings well up inside you, making your heart beat faster and harder.
But the various buildings, the leaf-like patterned decorations, and the gentle wind help calm your pulse.
Perhaps a little time in the city air isn't so bad. Your comrades can wait.

With no one to talk to and no orders to follow, you have no idea what to do.
So, like always, you simply wander, waiting for someone to give you orders.

Familiar roars echo in your ears, mingled with the voices of the lords and ladies in the distance. The banquet hall before you is the city residence of your roaring blue comrades.
You've been taken to places like this before, but only at the command of the lords and ladies. Coming here on your own feels new.
ㄚ— (Ah.)
ㄛˊ? (Oh?)
ㄣˋ! (Mhm!)
ㄏㄣˋ，ㄏㄣˊ (Mm-hmm.)
It's comfortable talking like this, familiar as ever. Chatting with your comrades passes some meaningless time here.
I saw Lyra too. Exactly how many are coming to this gathering?
Laurent Roseau invited just about everyone he knows—even Animus.
Animus? She loathes any gathering without the Guiding One present. I doubt she'll show her face.
She's already here. Laurent was quite boastful in his message ... Not that I care for his bragging—he asked something of me.

You listen to the two talk and realize you have stumbled upon a grand banquet, with even those who rarely show their faces in attendance. Not that it matters much, anyone taller than you is a lord or lady, right?
You know what grand banquets mean—a chorus of voices and more food than you could possibly eat.

Everyone looks busy preparing for the banquet, the cacophony of sounds creating an air of excitement.
You ignore them and walk between the tables and chairs in the hall.
Something forgotten in a corner becomes your reward for exploring.

You wander between your busy comrades, not sure what to do—like a moving bump in the road.
They shoo you off to a corner as if you were a fly.

Even when you move among your comrades, you feel like an outsider. Whether you stand still or move about, you're always wrapped in a judging gaze.
Now, surrounded, you face their close inspection.
Everyone here has a mission of some sort, and even an unexpected helper mustn't stay idle: "What can you do?"
Hm. That is the one thing you're any good at—sensing vibrations.
Go and find some new musicians in Paris for our orchestra, as you did before.

The little lady's words are encouraging. Her clear order sweeps away your confusion for now—you need only to obey, as you always do. You nod over and over, swinging your arms in a clear sign of acceptance.
You have been offered such grace, yet only wish to serve as the believer farthest from her, hm?
Fine, do as you will. But even in these trivial tasks, at least do not bring her shame. I know there are none who can truly serve her but me.
The tough lady's harsh, suffocating tone leaves you bewildered.
You don't know? Then leave. Don't stand in the way of those who are working.
He grabs you and carries you out of the banquet hall. And just like that, you escape their watchful eyes.
An angry mob approaches, chanting words you can't understand. Their anger seems to intermingle with the anger of the city, almost pulling you into their fervor.

They respond with loud shouts, mentioning strange phrases like "eight-hour workdays," "time off," and "benefits."
After listening carefully, you realize that they're rejecting orders simply because they dislike them. Unfathomable.

Though they're clearly speaking words, they sound more like the roars of your comrades.
You hear them, but can't make sense of what they're saying.

Whether out of curiosity or simply because you're caught up in the mood, you walk with them through the city, circling again and again. Except for the occasional stop in open squares, they never seem to tire.
After some time, and some decent exercise, you realize they aren't just wandering aimlessly like you. They're marching with a purpose—to protest the orders they've been given.

Whether out of curiosity or simply because you're caught up in the mood, you join them as they walk and shout. But, much like you, their movements seem to be aimless. Except for the occasional stop in open squares, they never seem to tire.
Your energy is no match for humans. In the end, you fail to keep up with their endless angry march.
An orchestra? Sure! Music will carry our voices farther than shouting ever could. Let's beat the drums and shake those hoity-toities off their pedestals!
Your left arm's performance connects with some members of the crowd, and they become your friends.
This is no time for art! We're fighting for tomorrow here!

Right now, their anger leaves no room for art. You're just glad their fury isn't aimed at you.
Still, they respond to your performance with a few kind words, and the warmth of them spreads across your face.
Jobs, huh? Well, that's what all this is about—better work. But we'll only take them if you meet every one of our demands ...
You manage to win over part of the marching crowd, and they become your friends.
Out of the way! Don't even think you'll buy me off! I'll never be a scab, and I won't betray the union!
They shout words you can't understand, push you aside, and keep marching on.
With the few words you know, you manage to convince some of the strikers to follow you without question.
They simply laugh and keep marching on.
Since the orders they're protesting have nothing to do with you, you decide to leave.
You show your power to the crowd, and most of them run away in fear. For some, however, that same fear drives them to follow you.
Your display of power can't convince them, and you can't understand their anger.
You can't convince them, nor understand their anger.

The absurd melody continues to spread, its roar infecting all around. Your left arm vibrates violently, as if it's channeling the thoughts of the entire city.
The strikers you spoke with earlier lose their humanity, slowly transforming into beast-like creatures, free from the constraints of commands and orders. Perhaps they've already conquered this "overtime" they've been chanting about.

Playing brings back memories of a loud, wordless past, as though those carefree days have returned to the city.
The growling beasts now feel like your comrades, straightforward and endearing.
You start to wonder if human language is necessary for you at all.

Chaos leads to bloodshed, and bloodshed risks lives. To protect people from harm, you decide to try something different from your comrades. You combine words with vibrations, using both to guide the crowd toward calm.
Under your direction, they become somewhat quieter, at least lowering their voices.

Chaos causes wounds, and wounds bring pain. To protect people from harm, you decide to try something different from your comrades.
But you don't know how to calm a crowd—no one ever taught you.

Slowly, you notice a strange dissonance in the city's melody—something different from the beasts' roars. You try to play the instrument on your arm, and although it feels strange, something in you instinctively knows how to join in.
It completely captivates you.
The strange dissonance comes from a group of people who ... appear to have no heads.
Their big hats completely obscure their faces, leaving you unsure of where they're looking.

Well, when it comes to the limits of intellect and order, I believe there's no need to repeat myself.
For the ritual to succeed, for our autonomy, the executor must meet the following requirements ...
You find the leader's complex speech hard to follow, but certain parts catch your attention, such as ...

Language is the symbol of socialization. Our executor must have been raised in an environment free from language, for this proves they remain untouched by humanity and thus possess an animalistic nature.
So, there must have been none who could speak among those who raised them ... No! Not any creature capable of communication at all!
All who serve a purpose in the universe are already bound in its chain of servitude. Our executor must be utterly useless and, therefore, truly free.
Precisely! We need someone entirely incapable of labor!
Independent thought, intellect—these aren't things an executor needs. Our executor must transcend thought. Only one who doesn't rely on thinking can break the boundaries of human understanding.
A being beyond logic! Inexplicably appearing in different times and places, appearing before us as if by fate!
You suddenly realize that every big hat is now staring directly at you, as if they just heard your thoughts.
Once again, you're surrounded—though by oversized hats this time—yet for some reason, you don't feel uneasy.
You try to sneak away, but there's already a big hat standing behind you.

The big hats offer you a comfortable chair and plenty of food in the room. Before you can even ask for it, whatever you need seems to appear in their hands. Everything you do or say garners nothing but cheers from them.

What a remarkable coincidence! The perfect ritual executor has appeared right before us!
I am—well, we're all curious ... what makes you who you are?
A brilliant answer!

Similar exchanges repeat over and over, with your every word and action met by cheers.
Then a knock interrupts, and the crab-faced lord you've seen before steps in carrying a weapon.
Headless ones, I come to fulfill our agreement on behalf of Manus Vindictae. I will perform your ritual, after which you will join—
Ah, no need for that now!
We've found the perfect executor! No need for any deals with you goo-drippers.
The big hats spread their arms, presenting you to the crab-faced lord, who sighs beneath his crab shell.

Coppélia, what are you doing here? ... No matter.
Since you have been chosen, you will perform their ritual.
And you, headless ones—our agreement stands.
Ah, no wonder that outfit of yours looked familiar. You're one of them, are you? A Manus?
A perfect answer! Then let's proceed with our original agreement, Manus Vindictae.
You follow the crab-faced lord and the big hats toward a massive gate far ahead.
We are nearly there, Coppélia. Just do as you agreed.
Ah, but first you must explain what she must do.
You didn't tell her?
To ensure the purity of the ritual, the executor must have no personal will, and neither must I. Otherwise the ritual will be contaminated by the limitations of thought.

Hah ... Listen carefully, Coppélia. When we reach the Arc de Triomphe, you will behead these people.
Can you manage that? If not, I will lend you my blade.

Don't worry, this is no mere suicide. To approach death is to touch its sacred nature.
Those born unfree must face death if they're to escape their duty as the mind and reason of the cosmos and claim sovereignty over the universe.
You, raised without thought or purpose, have always held this autonomy, which is precisely why you must be the one to lead this sacrifice!
At your age, you should be accustomed to such matters. The ritual requires some preparation. Go and sharpen your weapon.

You don't understand these words. A weapon? Beheading?
Why is the ritual not performed with music and song?
You find a spot where the sound is different. Suddenly, a strange, brightly colored animal pushes the stone aside, growls at you, and scurries away.
There's no time to chase it. But you find that the hole it left is large enough for you to crawl through.

The wall paint is peeling, and you notice a pattern. Some marks are only dirt, but others appear to be intentional markings.
You recognize a line of faded arrows. You're good at following those.
The arrows split in two directions. At the first arrow, you find a key, and at the second, you see a dusty locked box.

As you start to see the dim light outside, you spot a dusty box inside a hole in the wall.
It's locked.
Your foot catches on a chest hidden in the dark, and you fall. But as your hand sinks into the wet mud, it finds a key.
You struggle up from the ground, kick the railing aside and hear a clear clink—a locked box.
The lid clicks open. Drenched, you take the unexpected gift and leave.
The lid clicks open. The arrows continue ahead, and you follow them out of the magical pipe world.
You approach and begin evaluating your new, silent travel companions.

Choosing a new travel companion requires natural intuition. You listen closely to the various quiet sounds and find one that seems eager for your company.
It feels heavy and has a strange key attached.

In the silence, you hear little welcoming chirps.
Soon, a few Goldfinch Coins jump into your pocket, your new travel companions.

As usual, you shift seats to arrange your new companions and help them feel more comfortable.
Your new friends seem to appreciate how you've organized things.
A duet of shouts breaks the silence—one side attacking, one side pleading ... You look around and spot a high window above a locked door.
Standing in front of the salon, you hear a duet of shouts—one side shouting and the other pleading ... You look around and trace the cacophony to a high window above a locked door.
Your new companion helps you open the door. Now, the strange duet of aggression and fear within bursts forth clear and true.

The door is locked, so you use the window. With a firm grip, you pull yourself up.
Now, the strange duet of rage and fear within bursts forth clear and true.
Your painful yell adds to the duet as you struggle. It looks like you need a new plan or to give up.

After some fiddling, the lock opens.
Now, the strange duet of rage and fear within bursts forth clear and true.

Despite your best efforts to pick the lock like you were taught, it won't budge.
It looks like you need a new plan or to give up.
You like your salon friends and don't feel like joining another.

You discover the source of the strange melody—a miniature battle between two armies of tin soldiers. You smile as you produce the lone tin soldier you've been carrying; you've finally found him a home.

Food, coins, and toys are piled in an abandoned space.
They could be useful later, or maybe just nice to have. Either way, what you get depends on what you can carry.
You grab a few toys and listen as they make strange sounds.
You eat some of the food and find yourself less hungry.
You gather the coins you'll need for dealing with outsiders.
You don't even like tidying your own room, let alone bothering with this strange place.
Supplies remain plentiful, and you still want more.
You stuff toys into every pocket until their weight slows you down. Bigger pockets aren't always better.
You stuff your cheeks with food, but there's still more left. And you start to feel bad about letting any of it go to waste.
You grab coins until their mad jingling becomes dizzying; maybe there are downsides to being rich.

The owner of this strange space, a terrifying monster, returns. He says nothing but holds out his hand expectantly.
You're too burdened to run, and dropping your load isn't an option.
He charges what may or may not be fair, then carefully counts out your coins.
Since you are unwilling or unable to pay normally, the owner has decided to take your blood as payment and punish you with some added pain.

You reach a dead end and see a single door. It looks like it hasn't been used in a long time—its hinges are caked over with rust.
You could turn back, but you'll never know what's behind that door.
You push the door with all your strength. It screeches loudly, piercing your ears.
Opening a door shouldn't be this painful. You decide to give up.
You breathe deeply and put all your strength into the door. The screech grows louder still.
You step back and charge forward, ramming your weight into the door. The noise and pain are overwhelming.
You manage to open a gap wide enough to slip through. Something was blocking the door from the other side.
You clear the obstruction and claim it as your prize. The door opens, and the annoying noise leaves your mind.
You step over it and pass through. The door will soon close, but you're always getting lost, so what are the chances you'll ever be back?

You recognize the fragrance. It’s the same one from the notes she left for you. You listen carefully but don't hear her voice.
Her voice also carries a fragrance. Whenever you smell it, you avoid punishment, get candy, or hear things you don't fully understand.
Of course, protecting yourself is important. Some tasks cause pain, and pain is never good. You remember answering her like this.

You wake up, and the fragrance is gone. Clutched in your hand is a small glass bottle. It's the "trance." You recall her warning: indulging in her fragrance can harm your mind.
But it's given you what you need, once again.
The wind is cool, and the sun feels nice. You want to stay outside longer. You remember answering her this way.
I think I'm starting to understand what you said ... no, not quite yet ...
Rather than answer, you want to find her and ask her about those words.
You realize the space around you is still empty and silent—it's an illusion.

You recall her warning: her scent brings on the "trance."
She only appears when you truly need her. Maybe not now. You remember one of her notes. You should "go around" now.

Your sense of direction while wandering brings you back to the blue room.
Nothing has changed since you left. Though the sweet scent of nectar is nearly gone.

You sit on the floor, hugging your knees, enjoying the rare peace.
This solitude is yours alone, but the mindless state helps you carry the burden of your journey.

You decide now is the time to pick up your interrupted rest. You close your eyes, letting the warmth soothe you ...
Until the scent of nectar invades your nostrils, forcing you awake. The rich aroma piques your senses, preventing you from sinking back into the room's gloom.

A crack appears in the ground ahead, tripping you.
You lose your balance and fall. The pain makes you close your eyes briefly. When you open them again, you find yourself in a strange city.
You were just getting used to the last city, and now there's a new one to learn.

You notice a change in weight. You may have lost something when you fell.
You rummage through your pockets.
Thankfully, nothing is missing, though somehow everything looks different.
Absorbed in counting, you unknowingly return to the familiar city.

New things always interest you more than old ones. You soon realize this city is a treasure trove.
Various melodies fill the air, merging into a sea of sound.
You follow a few strands of melody and soon find yourself back in the original city.
But the melodies begin to fade, and no matter how hard you try, you can't recall them.
Getting lost isn't good, and this city feels empty without your comrades. You decide to find a way back immediately.
In your haste, you hear clear melodies guiding you. Soon, you're back where you fell.
But the memory of that city starts to blur, leaving only a metallic taste in your mouth and the melodies along the way vividly clear.
Your knees hurt from the fall, so you sit to rub them, easing the pain.
Time and pain pass, with the rhythmic pulse of your blood vessels forming an impressive melody.
You stand up and return to the streets of the city. The crack that tripped you is nowhere to be seen.
A spark of inspiration, a bit of courage, and maybe a little luck can help you see deeper into the world. Of course, a few Goldfinch Coins are also necessary.
You watch the artefact carefully as it shifts, eventually taking the form you were expecting.
You try every approach you can think of, but the artefact changes in ways you didn't anticipate.
Genius? What you're seeing is just hard work and perseverance.
You earnestly search for an answer. It isn't perfect, but it could be worse.
Something seems to have interfered with your work. It just feels off.
This isn't luck. It's the result of always sticking to the rules.

On the crowded street, you hear a cluster of trembling notes.
"—Mommy!"
You see a little girl crying in the middle of the road.

You reach into your pocket and hand the little human one of your treasured keepsakes.
She takes it, sniffling as she looks down at it, then bursts into even louder sobs. "Mommy—!"

You rummage through every pocket and pull out a few Goldfinch Coins. You've seen people stop crying for the sake of gold before. You lay them out before the tiny human.
But she cries even harder, flinging them away. The Goldfinch Coins clatter and tumble into the sewer below.

You take the little human's hand, trying to make sense of her tear-muddled words. She mentions "candy," "the park," and "Rue du Faubourg Honoré," and you decide to see if you can find anything for her.
Your mission is much more important than helping some crying child.

The sobbing little human clings to you. Your attempts to calm her do nothing until a shout comes from across the street.
The little human stumbles toward a figure wrapped in red cloth, who opens her arms to catch her.
Kind soul, please accept my thanks! May good fortune smile upon you!
Tears and smiles hang on her face at once, and you can't tell what she's really thinking.
She hands you a few chattering Goldfinch Coins and gives you an awkward hug before leaving.

The streets feel familiar. You remember meeting a crying child here.
You suddenly feel a primal sense of danger. You turn around—a knife comes hurtling toward you.

Before you can evade that looming shadow, a beast flashes by, dragging, tearing, and shredding it apart. The scream pierces your ears.
Even in the darkness, you know it isn't the sound of a beast. She—or he—nods to you once before leaving.

Before you can even get a word out, a beast flashes by, dragging, tearing, and shredding it apart. The scream tears through your ears.
Even in the darkness, you know it isn't the sound of a beast. She—or he—nods to you once before leaving.

Before you can react, a beast flashes by like lightning, dragging, tearing, and shredding the shadow apart.
Even in the darkness, you know it isn't the sound of a beast. She—or he—nods to you once before leaving.

You instinctively raise your arm to block the shadow, but it doesn't stop. Then a beast flashes by, lunging at the shadow and ripping it apart.
The beast tears through what's left of their belongings, paying you no mind, and even tosses something heavy your way.

The street band's music grabs your attention. Many others pause too.
Maybe this is a good time to recruit some local talent.

You start to conduct the ensemble. Their music wraps around you. Everything flows, graceful and in tune.
The performers are in awe of you. They believe your arrival is a sign—
You're the one who'll make them be heard.
Everyone's got their own taste in music—or so they think. Some nod at you; others cover their ears and walk off.

But your music is drowned out by the noise of the city.
Only a scant few passersby notice your melody, and most of them keep walking.
Not every echo finds an audience.

You follow the crowd into a hall with a transparent dome. Paintings cover the walls. Praise, sighs, and chatter fill the air.
Among the chatter, you hear beautiful words—perhaps you can make some friends, depending on what you say.
You nod, repeating bland affirmations that never fail in adult conversations, blending seamlessly into the chatter.
You've rarely spoken so fluently. People praise your firsthand tales as "thought-provoking parables" and line up to shake your hand.
Your words spark laughter, and the crowd around you grows—maybe you're quite popular after all.
You bite your tongue tripping over a complex word. By the time the pain subsides, the chatter has long faded away.
There are too many people here, and the words they use are far too complicated. Your throat feels tight.

You see a folded sign reading—
"Coffee is the fuel for socialization, creativity, and thought. The choice of intellectuals and artists alike."
If you're looking for comrades, you'll find them among the artists—you remember an expert's advice.
The shade of the plants makes you feel at ease. Many others share the same thought, and to keep the warmth alive, they strike up a conversation with you.

It surprises you.
Someone has prepared the food so beautifully it seems like a crime to eat it. 
You don't have to do much to tell apart the starving from the artists. Soon enough you find plenty of kindred spirits.

It surprises you.
Someone has prepared the food so beautifully it seems like a crime to eat it. 
You can't quite tell the starving from the artists, but you still manage to find a few kindred spirits.
The brown drink makes your head throb as if it were swelling up like a balloon. Perhaps it was a poison meant to keep you away.

A car screeches with a chaotic honk and veers toward the lawn to the side. The rhythm of it all is almost comical, so you follow the sound to the street corner ...
"Git outta th' way!" A group of Critters driving the car are heading straight for you. This is dangerous.
Your left hand shields you and also crushes the car. The remaining Critters are furious.
Your left hand softens the impact, and both you and the car topple over. The Critters don't seem happy about it.

Their repetitive rhythm is easy to predict. You sidestep the Critters' charge.
They slam straight into a roadside tree. The car's wrecked, and the remaining Critters look ready to take out their frustration on you.

You fail to dodge the speeding car, but your left hand cushions the blow just in time.
Both you and the car topple aside, and the Critters are none too pleased.

You lose your way in a mist and find yourself in a forest. A cave appears through the canopy.
Thick grass, clear water, moist air—muddy underfoot, but a fine place to sleep.
Unfortunately, something's claimed it first.
You try to drive them off with strength, which only makes them more alert.
They realize you're much tougher than them and they start searching for a chance to flee.
They show no fear, deciding you are weak and therefore easy prey.
Your comrades launch a surprise attack, and you follow suit, striking before the Critters can react.
You mimic your comrades' silent attack, but the Critters are faster. They spot your rash move and turn it against you.
A battle with the Critters begins over ownership of this den.

Roars fill your ears. People are marching in protest.
When you notice the beasts among them, it's too late—they've surrounded you, and in the chaos, their hostility turns towards you.
You crush a beast before you with full force, but more beasts keep coming.
You lack the power to fell the beast in one strike, and even more are closing in.
You try to bring order back to the chaotic rhythm. The beasts calm down a little, but there are too many of them to control.
You try to bring order back to the chaotic rhythm, but the beasts don't listen, and their numbers keep growing.
You choose the path with the fewest beasts, hoping to break through with minimal pain and effort.

"Some cleverer people are already handling this, but I'm really short-handed. I can offer you this much."
He raises one finger.

"You're a lifesaver! I'll give you this much."
He raises two fingers.

"Really? No one usually takes these! It's worth this much!"
He raises three fingers.

You recognize some words, but the sentences on these papers confuse you.
You turn to leave, ignoring him calling out to you from behind.
You copy his gesture by raising your own fingers—a new way to communicate.

"Of course, of course—desperate times call for reasonable requests!"
He smiles, nods, raises a few more fingers, and shows you out.

"Hmm ... I think my offer is fair enough."
He shakes his head and shows you out.
You reach out and touch his hand—supposedly a greeting, but he seems surprised.

"Hmm ... Alright, alright! Desperate times call for desperate measures!"
He reluctantly high-fives you with his other hand and shows you out.

"If you don't want the job, just say so. I need to consider costs ..."
He snatches the paper back and pushes you out.

"Goodbye! Good luck!"
He waves you out the door. You try to pick out a few familiar sentences from the papers.

Your comrade responds with sharp, quick roars. It's clear he's new and still doesn't understand the lords' and ladies' tasks.
Few know less than you—curious, you lean in a little closer.
The comrade then grabs you, asking for help with his tasks.

You know it's better not to disturb a comrade who's working or ask what he was told.
You remember a lord or lady telling you to stay out of others' business, so you quietly walk away, leaving the comrade's sound behind.

The comrade now seems overwhelmed with multiple tasks.
He insists that you help with at least one of them.

Things turn out worse than expected. You've never heard of these tasks and don't know how to handle any of them.
You decide to run off rather than struggle together.

You follow the example of your previous comrade, handing over the duties entrusted to you to the one now in front of you.
The new comrade growls and agrees right away.

You follow the example of your previous comrade, handing over the duties entrusted to you to the one now in front of you.
The new comrade grumbles. Since you're not a lady, he demands something to help.

You follow the example of your previous comrade, handing over the duties entrusted to you to the one now in front of you.
The new comrade moves his arms angrily. Since you're not a lady, he demands something valuable to help.
You no longer worry about the tasks. Asking for help has worked well, and now you feel relieved.
You decide it's wrong to pass your troubles onto others. You say goodbye and try to handle the task yourself, even though it wasn't yours in the first place.

You greet your comrade warmly, but he walks off too.
It feels like you missed an opportunity to avoid trouble.
Are you just hanging around?
... She gives you too much freedom, but if you really can be useful and do what is asked of you by the Guiding One, I guess I can't complain.

You lower your head and say you'll walk the streets of the city.
She nods, then shakes her head.
Not enough.

You lower your head and say you'll help other comrades finish their tasks.
She nods, then shakes her head.

You lower your head and say you'll follow her orders.
She nods, then shakes her head.

You don't fully understand what "being useful" means.
She watches you, shakes her head, stops talking, and walks away.

You realize she expects you to do more.
Maybe you need to think harder about how you can be useful.
The notes in your room don't provide clues, so you make a random guess. She frowns, still not satisfied.
You recall the usual tasks your comrades perform and name a goal. She pauses, nods, but still seems unsatisfied.
You remember some discussions between the lords and ladies in the banquet hall and name a goal. She nods but asks you to elaborate.

The notes in your room don't provide clues, so you space out.
When you snap back to attention, the tough lady is gone.
You don't know what to say, so you repeat what your comrades say when concluding an audience with lords and ladies, hoping the long conversation ends soon.

She sighs, gives you simple tasks, and lets you go.
You run off and decide never to return.

She nods, gives you moderately difficult tasks, and lets you go.
You run off and decide never to return.

She finally smiles, gives you complex orders, and lets you go.
You run off and decide never to return.
She looks confused and doesn't understand your words. You step back and then run, deciding never to come back.
You're carrying too much and feel weighed down. You eagerly stuff Goldfinch Coins into the lion's mouth and feel lighter.
You feel the lion is less friendly than the talking painting. You cover your ears and close your pockets, getting away from it as soon as possible.
You look inside the lion's mouth and see black fur. Leaning closer, you look between the teeth and spot round eyes with narrow pupils.

You believe that the Critter won't affect the lion.
You're carrying too much and feel weighed down. You eagerly stuff Goldfinch Coins into the lion's mouth and feel lighter.

You grab the Critter by its fur, yanking it out before it has a chance to bite. 
The Critter yells in the lion's voice, but you don't stop. From the lion's now-silent mouth—the Critter's former nest—you pull out a few other valuable things, all covered with its fur.
The eyes scare you. You cover your pockets and leave, wary of the lion with eyes in its mouth.
You meet the talking stone lion again. As promised, it gives you more Goldfinch Coins than you initially deposited, without any of the lion's saliva you feared.
Squeak! Mane's Bank at your service! You now owe 5000 Goldfinch Coins. Your repayment deadline is ... Want a withdrawal? Sorry, no coins until you pay off your loan!
A Critter peeks from the lion's mouth, squeaks triumphantly, and dives back in again.

Inside, you feel the cold, narrow stone walls. You wrestle a fuzzy thing with sharp little teeth.
You punch the fuzzball—it screeches and stops biting.
Victorious and undisturbed, you're free to take everything from the Critter's stone den.

Inside, you feel the cold, narrow stone walls. You wrestle a fuzzy thing with sharp little teeth.
It bites your hand hard. You yell and pull back.
Now you have traded 150 Goldfinch Coins for a hurt hand. Not worth it! You leave, sulking.

The closer you draw to the room, the more the joyous and somber melodies intertwine. The dancers' arms cut through the air, leaving a blur of shadows. Outside the window, time seems to warp—one moment it is day, the next, moonlight glows. The scene feels familiar enough to draw you near, yet strange enough to make you want to run away.
You enter the room. Your arm begins to hum with the instruments in the corner, and your surroundings change like the shifting light outside the window. Your legs start to sway along with the crowd.
You feel both happy and miserable as you stumble toward a spot to unwind.

You understand instruments more than anything else, so you decide to sit by the musicians. You recognize the guitar, violins, and double bass. Their warm quintet blends with your own vibrations.
A strange feeling hits you. Suddenly, the crowd in the room vanishes.

You look outside and see streets you've just walked through. The sight reminds you of where you are, but you then spot a similar building in the sky that disappears quickly.
A strange feeling hits you. Suddenly, the crowd in the room vanishes.

They welcome you warmly. Talking excitedly about the tune—mentioning "Gibsie" and "sy-jazz."
Ten hands reach for you, ten pairs of eyes watch you closely.
A strange feeling hits you. Suddenly, the crowd in the room vanishes.

You shake your head, trying to focus, and notice unusual vibrations in the fur-covered dancers.
You shake their shoulders, shouting, but the dance wave pushes you back.
Dizzied, you look up, and the strange crowd in the room is gone.

You're not sure what happened, but it was confusing, like many things today.
You decide to leave, thinking it might be best to forget what you just experienced.

A comrade once told you that remembering too much can drive a person mad.
"Mad" sounds scary, so you decide to stop thinking about it altogether.

The one who left you notes told you that memory is like the sweet wine of life.
"Sweet wine" sounds good, so you decide not to forget anything easily.

You wander into a room where someone is pacing, just like you do when you're bored and alone.
He sees you and smiles.
"Finally, someone! What can you do?"
He spreads out a stack of papers covered in writing, seemingly waiting for you to pick one.

You hear a sound nearby, different from the usual singing of your comrades. Its sound is a confused and lonely solo.
Following the sound, you find a triangular comrade walking in circles.
The banquet hall is inside a massive building, leading you to wander through its endless hallways and rooms. You enjoy opening doors, but this time, you attract the attention of a tough lady.

A talking stone lion stops you and claims to be an ATM for Mane's Bank. It offers loans, withdrawals, high-interest savings, and more.
After it explains several times, you understand it's like the talking painting in the banquet hall. You can leave Goldfinch Coins you don't want to carry and retrieve more later.
You encounter the talking stone lion once again.

A beautiful melody lures you to the door of a spacious room. People are dancing in pairs, spinning and twirling, their coats and skirts fluttering as they move. Some of them are covered in shimmering fur.

You follow a horde of people into the house.
They sit in small groups with books, newspapers, canes, or teacups in hand, talking quietly among themselves.
Someone carrying a tray walks up and politely asks what you'd like.
You're exhausted from your journey, and you make a beeline for the couch in the corner.

Safe, soft, perfect for resting.
You slowly sink into the cushions, your head lowering more and more until it brushes the fabric, and you fall asleep.
After an uninterrupted nap, you wake up feeling like you could walk the length of the city twice over.

You ignore the server and head toward the small groups, curious what they're talking about.
But the moment you step closer, the conversations stop, and someone waves the server over.
A moment later, another smiling staff member walks up, slips a few coins into your hand, and, together with the server, gently ushers you out the door.

You figure that "holding something" must be some rule everyone in this room follows, so you take the tray of food.
Sure enough, no one ushers you out. You wander around with the tray in hand and overhear all sorts of conversations, half of which you only vaguely understand, but all of which sound interesting.

You pat your pocket, fish out a key you found on the road, and hand it to the server.
He seems to recognize it and respectfully leads you upstairs to a nicer room filled with curious decorations, completely devoid of people.

They seem to be letting you rest here. You flip through a book of incantations on the desk, take sips from strange bottled liquids on the shelf, and fiddle with a metal device puffing out strange little clouds.
Eventually, you curl up on the silk-covered bed and take a nap, slipping out the window after you wake.

A beast bursts out from its lair, opening a new space for you.
The room is a wreck—fallen picture frames, blankets, cramped cabinets, wax frozen on the floor ... clearly not an ideal place to rest, but no reason to rush off either.

The fire lights up the room, and something shiny in the corner catches the glow, reflecting vivid colors.
The beast won't mind if you take it.

These are portraits. Their expressions hook your curiosity—some smiling, some unhappy, some looking even scarier than the lords and ladies.
You lose yourself in the paint and the strokes, as if you're talking to the portraits without saying anything.
A strange, pleasant feeling washes over you, sticking around in your subconscious.

Doing what you've seen friends do most often when scavenging, you start opening drawers.
Everything inside is intact. When you pick it up, you remember what the kind lady once told you: people always hide their treasures somewhere sturdy.
The beast no longer cares about it, but you can take it and look after it.
Beneath the carpet is a trapdoor. You lift it and crack it open just enough to peek inside—then a surge of force blasts through the gap, sending a puff of brilliant beast fur into the air.

The hairs rub against each other, ringing like a hundred instruments at once, the room echoing with countless overlapping sounds ... and when it all fades, some of the melodies still linger in your ears.

Rather than you locking an enraged beast outside, it feels more like you've locked yourself in.
The door is sturdy enough to save you from claws and teeth, but you'll need to find a way out eventually.

Maybe there's another way out at the end of this path.
With that hope in mind, you head deeper—only to run into a group of Critters before you find the exit.

You decide to sit and rest before making a plan.
Time slips away quickly when you're lost in thought.
Before you can figure out anything useful, the scraping of claws against the door stops—it seems like the danger wandered off on its own.
The Critters scatter toward the depths. Maybe they know where the exit is.

The light dims, and you're left relying on sound and touch to guide you forward.
Then, beneath your footsteps and the distant dripping of water, you hear a low, ominous growl.
Time passes as you retrace your steps. When you return to the door, everything outside is silent. Looks like the danger left on its own.

You defeat the creature.
As it collapses, it crashes into something. Stone crumbles, debris falls, and a faint light appears in the distance.

Looks like this is the second exit you were hoping to find. Unfortunately, it's not just an exit, it's someone's nest.
And judging from how it reacts to the tremors, it's very clear your presence is the last thing it wants.

Matilda once told me about the Suitcase's ever-shifting terrain.
But seeing it myself, I must admit—it is far more intriguing than any words could capture.
A place of unpredictable change: mountain slopes today, running water tomorrow ...
Vertin, how many mysteries lie hidden in this place?
I should have visited sooner.
Oh, but I do not. I have had some truly ... new experiences.
Yesterday, I got lost for the very first time.
And for the very first time, I asked someone for directions. I asked several people. Everyone had a different guess.
I mean no complaint; it was a very engaging half hour indeed.
Of course, not everyone appreciates the concept of "getting lost."
Adèle once planned to return to her old craft here in the Suitcase.
But with all these changes, it will not be easy to achieve.
I found this by a pond.
Do you recognize it? There was a group of Critters chirping around it at the time.
So it really is a dragon?!
Feufeu's been eager to breathe fire on it.
It seems he doesn't quite believe his kin would leave behind nothing but bones.
Do you say that because you're confident it's real, or because you're also unsure? Allow me to hazard a guess ...
Hmmm, non. I can't tell from your face at all ...
Alright then. Let's see whether it turns to ash, or—
Ohh, Vertin! You've got the real thing.
Can you believe it? An authentic dragon bone, just lying beside a pool of water! Bon sang, any adventurer would be giddy over this place.
Heh ... These days, the children have been querying me over the winner of the coming matches.
It is this "Critter Crash" game they play.
They tell me you are quite a formidable opponent, Vertin. Many place their bets on you.
Then you, too, wish for an early answer. I am afraid ...
I must refuse to foresee it.
The answer would spoil the fun—for players and watchers alike.
Allow me this small enjoyment of the unknown, will you? I have already booked my seat for the finals.
Is that so? Then her determination to win is little wonder.
Whenever the children come to me about it, Matilda finds a reason to slip away.
A mother knows her daughter. I do not believe she would divine such a thing.
Matilda is a determined young woman. She will doggedly chase her goals, no matter the answers given.
Not even the unpredictable "Storm" has changed that about her.
Vertin! Here, I prepared an invitation for you.
Sender: me. Destination: ... my trunk!
Do you have a moment to take a look?
Ever since you first told me to step into this Suitcase, I've been thinking.
The invitation was intriguing, but what I found inside the Suitcase was astounding.
Preparing a gift to match it was ... troublesome, to say the least.
So I've prepared a little surprise in the trunk of my car. It somewhat resembles "stepping into a suitcase," n'est-ce pas? How about it? Want to try?
Let me think ... left foot first?
Hahaha, no, no. Just go ahead and open it.
Before I'd stepped into your Suitcase, I couldn't have possibly imagined it being so vast inside—my trunk isn't nearly so magical.
Promise me you won't be disappointed by what's inside because of that—oh! Did I just spoil it?
It's still largely unexplored
No need to exaggerate for my sake
It has its inconveniences too
It's a Wyrmling skeleton
Let him test it
So ... will I win?
Matilda's good at it too
Could Matilda divine the results too?
Your trunk?
How?

Do you really believe you can escape this? Escape me?
Soldiers ... shapeshifting ... Manus Vindictae?
My dear, foolish Adèle ... You are but a grain of sand before the tides of fate.
What good could possibly come from fighting me?
The rift is widening. We have to stop her.
Those monsters ... they're forming some sort of shield. We need to break through ...
Allez, Adèle, think!
Leave me alone, you ... phantoms!
If the Depths of Myth is nothing more than a sea of collective unconscious, then the creatures born from it must be ...
... mere reflections!
Is that feeble little flame supposed to scare me?
Open your eyes and look around—can you not see what these miserable people want?
I am Félicienne, she who defies death—the one true existence among you short-lived creatures!
Who are you to think you can stop me?
I'm nobody. Just a tour guide from Paris who can handle a car—and tell truth from lies!
By fire, what is false is purged!
*panting*
Stop this, Félicienne.
You're no master of this city. You're not even the master of yourself.
Vive L'Empereur! The free men of Paris will never be defeated by the likes of you!
Hey! I'm a free woman of Paris too—I'm on your side!
Lies! You're nothing but a lapdog of the aristocracy! A blight on our society! A parasite to all of France!
I think you need to calm down, monsieur!
Professor Roseau ... what have you done?!
I had wanted this to be a surprise, Célia. Our research has entered a new phase.
A new phase? All I saw was Vincent turning into a monster!
Hush ... no need to get so worked up. All he has done is assume the form his subconscious most desired. Isn't that right, Vincent?
*growl*
This is madness ...
Please, Célia, let us resolve this misunderstanding civilly.
Don't you see—Vincent gained a body far superior to the one he'd had before. And let's be honest, he wasn't my most exceptional student.
But you—you have the potential to be so much better. Through the Depths of Myth, you can be freed from this flawed mortal shell!
Come, Célia. It's time you took the step that will change the world.
Stay away from me, you lunatic!
What a pity, Célia. You had such promise.
You truly are my finest pupil. Must I treat you as I did Vincent to make you see?
This will be a tragic loss ... for my academic legacy.
Must you crash the party in such a barbaric fashion, Adèle?
What happened to my body? What did you do to me?!
Enough questions. This body is mine now.
It comes with some amusingly useless arcane skills, but I suppose I could do worse.
From this day forward, this body will serve only my noble soul. You ought to feel honored.
Get out of my body!
This was a shameful display, Laurence Roseau.
The outcome was far from unexpected. Taira, now lower that weapon. I'm still observing this fascinating turn of events.
Señor Roseau's research wasn't all roses either ... Hmm, where did Animus go?
She left in a great huff, something about "blasphemy."
Apparently, she had no patience left for "this farce."
How utterly stubborn can you be?!
This false era is ending. If you intend to continue to exist in the one to come, you must surrender your body to me!
I'm done listening to you order me around. You may think it "amusingly useless," but let's see how you handle my fire.
Ugh, you barbarian!
Tut! How much longer do you intend to play around with that cursed flame?!
Not long, just until you leave my body—for good.
Enough ... Enough!! You're fired, Adèle!
Took you long enough.
You did well! Hit it again! Hit it again!
At last, we'll have a complete life ... hm?
You still have a chance to back out. Don't throw your life away.
You listened to those headless ramblings and want to chase death too?

The Thousandfold Fate

Each drop of water a ripple of fate,
Melting beneath her bright, fragile gaze.
One thousand ripples, one thousand creases,
Yet one remains, unmelting, ceaseless.
—A drop of fallen blood.
Her Willful Leap

Born to be free, we are fish in water,
Born to drift, we are boats on a river,
Torn by the tempest, our vessels we'll shed,
Naked we'll drown—
Or we'll leap the riverbed.
Shadows in the Subconscious

It rests in my pupils, runs in my veins,
Crying, laughing, whispering my name.
It beats in my heart and wanders my mind,
An unspeakable bond—what's yours and what's mine.
For we share one shadow—one body, two souls,
An inseparable bond: two people, one whole.
In Their Figures

Reflections capture every embrace, 
but they cannot recount the fullness of the moment. 
The warmth of arms, the lift of brows, the quiet breaths—
we exist here, as the truth beyond the reflection.
