The Sharpest Blade

Forged from high-carbon steel, a double-edged blade and handle shaped from a single billet. Nearly twenty inches in length, yet it weighs only one pound and seven ounces—light in the hand, deadly in use.
You would not want to see an enemy pull out a blade like this from twenty paces away. The fine engravings and ornamentation are charming, but all of that is nothing compared to its honed edge.
It has served for many years, tended with meticulous care, and it has earned its place as a trusted companion—a gift given with ceremony upon adulthood.
Lucky Charm

May misfortune pass you by, and may enemy bullets and blades never reach you. May you skim the plains like an eagle, and then soar toward the horizon, not losing even a single feather. May your courage bring victory, for we will pray to the gods on your behalf. For ages unending, the sun and moon watch over the land and guard your health and your peace. And one day, as you depart now, so too shall you return to us.
The Last Crescent Moon

The crescent once worn on his left ear is now a keepsake, a memento. And the moment his kin see it, they will understand.
A people that values families, they believe bravery runs in their blood, and that the shashka grants them unstoppable strength. But not everyone possesses such physical might. Incantations and spells can rarely stop bullets. His proud steed fell under a single slash, and his life was no match for a bullet to the brow. Yet neither he nor his people would ever regret riding into battle with shashkas drawn, chasing death head-on.
The last crescent moon waits to return home, to cross the vast steppe with his kin, to taste freedom again on the wind, and finally knock on his family's door, coming home to where his bloodline began.
A Carefully-Sewn Home

Your mother's last letter held her longing and blessings for you, and I feel the same, so I will keep this short. You know I am not good at writing letters. A few years ago, I was like you, always on the road.
Your mother worked hard to make this felt mat. It is soft, elegant, and should match the saddle I crafted for you before you left. I taught you to ride, so you know well enough how important the saddle is. Whatever fine steed you ride now, take care of it. Do not let its back chafe raw and bleed.
Next time, you should receive felt boots and a short coat. I saw your mother measuring—or, more precisely, imagining—your current height. To spare her some worry, send your measurements in your next letter—yes, I am telling you to write home. Do not forget.
Golden Waves of Wheat

I know no one wants to hear babbles, and I do not enjoy writing babbles either, so I will be direct: the wheat is growing great this year. Planting season has only just ended, yet the fields are already turning gold. Give it a little longer and we will surely have a fine harvest.
When you return, you will be eating the best bread, I promise ... though it reminds me of old Anton. He said the wheat is growing too fast—eighty years of life and he had never seen anything like it. Grisha joked it was because he hadn't lived long enough, and earned himself a whipping. Anton may be old, but his temper is as sharp as ever, and he can still swing a shashka well enough to silence any teasing. That said, he claimed it was some kind of omen and insisted we send the kolduny in the village to take a look.
All right, I have babbled, after all. If you read this far, thank you. Truth be told, I'm already waiting for that bread myself. You truly—truly have nothing to worry about at home.

"It exists, I swear it does! Look, right here—inside my flesh, inside my organs." The offering-bearer raised his shredded hands high, still smiling. Yes, even without eyes, he was still smiling. For he longs to become a part of it.
"Countless moths, nameless moths—they drowned the sun and moon in darkness. They drowned themselves as well." Until the cocoon is complete, do not expect anything from what rests inside.
"Truth. I saw the truth—so pure, so beautiful. Look, look, everything I sought now has an answer!" At last, here and there, they shed "chaos" and became part of "order."

In an old bookstore on Rue Saint-Honoré, a faded book draws your attention. Its contents are exactly what you want to understand. You brush your fingers once more across the gold-stamped title.
Salon Etiquette—Written by a Court Attendant
Yes. A book that helps you blend into society.
The Beasts of North Africa
Yes. A book that awakens the wild.
The Lover Holding Lilies
Yes. A book that lights two souls at once.
Elements of Geometry
Yes. A book that questions the nature of the world.
A masquerade ball is taking place in Montmartre. It lacks a clear theme, but a mask is required for entry. So you pick up:
A polished silver mask with a polite smile
Everyone must appear proper.
A rough wooden mask carved with totem motifs
A mask can be "natural" too.
An enamel mask adorned with multicolored feathers
Beauty is always compelling.
A lifelike paper mask painted to match your face
Pretend, for now, that you are still yourself.
Chants from marches and protests echo through the streets. You begin thinking about the roots of this era's unrest. Those surges of fear, anxiety, and anger—perhaps they come from:
The collapse of morals and the decay of the human heart.
Vile people with no sense of virtue.
A crisis of civilization and primal aggression.
Monkeys wearing clothes, nothing more.
A breakdown of connection and distance between people.
No one truly understands anyone else.
A world out of order and a universe out of balance.
Maybe the gods have lost their minds.
A kind friend sends you a fortune-telling postcard, saying the pattern on the back reveals your fate for the week. You flip it over and see:
Soft, winding curves.
Curling around every solitary nail.
Sharp, angular lines.
Even the paper seems stung.
A square missing one corner.
Still a square, as you can tell.
A full circle.
The most complete, most flawless pattern.

You're just about to enjoy your Mont Blanc and a rich cup of coffee when the argument at the next table gets louder. They're bothering you, sure, but one person's view does strike you as the more reasonable one:
"Those who withdraw from society are running from their responsibilities."
Not much different from exile.
"There is no evil, only good that society has yet to recognize."
Standards are always shifting.
"A lover is the part of yourself that got lost among humankind."
Ah, the romantic flair.
"One must realize they were whole from the very beginning."
So what are we even chasing.
Before a shop window on the Champs-Élysées, you stop for a long time, so long you don't notice the sky changing. What you're staring at is:
A Klein-blue gown flowing with black liquid.
You have to admit, it's impeccable taste.
A restored illustration of ancient Critters.
Were they always this noisy?
A smoking pipe cut clean in half.
Makes you wonder where the other half is shown.
An astronomical clock with its hands reversed.
There must be a deeper metaphor.
The Self You Portray

The entire history of humankind lives inside the human mind—what we call "racial memory." Over time, these shared memories condense into four "archetypes." Through their imagery and expression comes the "collective unconscious."

According to your assessment, your inner core resonates most strongly with the Persona.

You adapt to every era.
Decorum and social instinct are your tools; only the citadel of order can hold back the collapse of chaos, can't it? Even though relying on crumbling structures is risky, there is always another social role waiting to take you in for a while. Layer upon layer of masks—you don't mind being the hero or the clown, the sage or the fool. You are you, and you are the multitude.
Remember: a masked person gains an identity but loses their own face.

The Self You Unify

You are every era.
To pursue the center and totality of the personality is to pursue the Self. No matter how turbulent the world becomes, you yearn for a higher-dimensional, more primordial, more eternal order. Inner harmony and cosmic harmony are, in truth, the same thing. To reach that place, anything may be carried out—or abandoned. You are you, and you are the sum of all ages.
Remember: transcendence in higher dimensions often demands sacrifice in lower ones.

While doing research in the library, Tennant comes across records showing that the Tavernier family once owned a very rare gemstone. She stays up all night going through the archives to try and track it down, but her search turns up nothing.
Click shows the battlefield photos he took, and Charon touches them gently, as if he can still smell the sulfur and earth in the pictures.
Sentinel pulls out her last sealed military ration from her pocket. She takes one bite before drinking four or five mouthfuls of water.
At dusk, Fatutu meets 37 on the beach. After talking, they decide to take a walk on the beach together. When they make a pinky promise, both remember many things about the beach.
Loggerhead forgets to set the oven timer, which causes thick smoke to fill the kitchen. Bunny Bunny then gives her a long-term"kitchen ban."
As Matilda describes the scene, Sentinel slowly rebuilds the image of Place Saint-Michel in her mind and starts to miss the cafés there.
After enjoying dozens of days in the sun, Flutterpage gets a healthy tan and creates a deeper bond with Leilani.
Because of a clock malfunction, Oliver Fog leaves work 2 minutes later than usual. He carefully records the time as evidence for use in future time-off claims.
On this day in 1959, the Antarctic Treaty was signed. "Fluffy Duke," "Scarlet Titan," and "Brother Jake" are always in high spirits on this day.
Charlie played both Napoleon and Napoleon III on stage, her own way of paying homage to the emperors.

In 1910, neon light made its public debut at the Paris Motor Show. From that first rudimentary, red glow would evolve a spectrum of dreamlike hues, destined to illuminate the streets for an entire century.
Windsong could never thank Sotheby enough for her nutrient potion "Lady No. 500," which kept her going through the long winter field survey.
In 1930, All Quiet on the Western Front was released. Many years later, Charon sat alone in Noire's screening room and watched it in stoic silence.
In 1957, Vanguard TV-3 managed a heroic 1.2 meters before falling back and exploding. Sputnik reportedly offered her condolences.
A rare arcane bacterium was identified. Reports suggested that the colder the environment, the faster it feeds on food.
In 1968, the computer mouse was introduced to the public. Before that, X had his own experiment with pointing devices using a bowling ball as the trackball.
In 1957, Illiac Suite, the first score ever composed entirely by computer, was completed. John Titor showed great interest in it, while Barcarola felt it lacked a human touch.
The Statute of Westminster was enacted on this day in 1931, a foundational law for the modern Commonwealth.
On this day in 1901, the first radio signal was successfully transmitted across the Atlantic Ocean. Even today, the thought of this achievement still makes Ms. Radio's heart flutter with excitement.
Nautika joining the field survey significantly reduces travel expenses. A change that greatly pleases Windsong.
On this day in 1773, 342 chests of black tea were hurled into the sea. This also marks the day that the sirens in Boston Harbor were able to sample tea from Wuyi, China.
On the first day of Saturnalia, Druvis III conjures an evergreen tree at the children's request.
Ulrich quickly steps in to prevent some Laplace employees from using 32K memory disks to commemorate the release of the IBM 7090, pointing out how utterly inefficient and impractical the idea is.
Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol was first published on this day in 1843. Oliver Fog knows the story very well.

On this day in 1983, China introduced its first self-designed supercomputer, Yinhe-1 to the world. Madam Z sent a card to a schoolmate who contributed to its development, expressing her happiness for their achievement.
Near the end of Saturnalia, Shamane made small sculptures made of evergreen wood for everyone. Buddy Fairchild was happy to help him gather the raw materials using his front teeth.
Inspired by an ad from another soft drink brand, Regulus persuaded Jessica to pull a sleigh as she gave away cans of Dr. Papper.
The movie The Exorcist was released in theaters in 1973. Blonney strongly disapproved of the director firing guns during takes to get real reactions from the actors.
Flutterpage has been happy to help deliver letters between two pen pals living in the suitcase, even if the trip only takes about 30 seconds.
Pavia immediately gave up his plan to toughen himself for blows when he found out Spathodea would be his practice partner.
On this day in 1924, Edwin Hubble announced the discovery of the Andromeda Galaxy. Sometimes, Voyager can be seen looking at its direction.
With the catchy tune of Love Me Do looping in the background, Vertin had an undisturbed, quiet day.

Hissabeth burns a CD of Voyager's violin performance, hoping that someday it will be launched into space like the Voyager Golden Records.

It turns out Phil, the famous groundhog who predicts the weather on Groundhog Day, is actually a Critter—a purple squirrel, which explains why people think it's been the same groundhog making predictions since 1887.
Jealous of Luna 9's moon landing, Sputnik is secretly saving for a rocket of her own to return to space.

After a Manus Vindictae member botched a high-altitude landing with a "Short-Distance Safety Paraglider," Eternity, the one who had arranged its purchase, promised to provide additional safety training.
Bette finally quit her physically demanding role in a horror movie after several failed attempts. She was tired of contorting her body trying to play a character possessed by a ghost.

A new cookbook series titled "Special Cuisine" has landed on shelves, featuring titles like How to Cook Dirt and How to Cook Shamirs. It was written by an arcanist with the goal of helping people eat during hard times.
Pandora Wilson read an issue of Arcanist's Digest and felt it was too dry. Yet she appreciated its wide range of subjects and fresh marketing, saying UTTU should take notes.
While Cristallo read Little Red Riding Hood to everyone in the Wilderness, Rabies dozed off on a haystack, snoring away.
During a routine checkup, Ulrich chatted excitedly about a new Mersenne prime. Mesmer Jr., however, couldn't have cared less.

Recoleta struggles to keep up with Marcus's unnaturally quick reading speed. She's been forcing herself to write faster to meet "reader demand"—despite Marcus always saying that she needs ample time to digest a page.
Sweetheart got an offer to star in the movie The Grand Age of Entertainment.
Leilani couldn't answer the questions on her history test about her home, Hawaii. The examiner from Zeno had no choice but to fail her.
It's Ms. Radio's special day today. Her companions in the Suitcase surprised her with a gift of blue zinnias.
Necrologist spoke with a couple's tombstones and learned they had died with no regrets. As it turned out, their lack of regrets meant she got an extra day off.
An LSCC researcher presents a hypothesis: Manus Vindictae's enigmatic black substance could be leveraged as a foundational material to engineer autonomous arcane artefacts.
A new vampire film, An Unfinished Dream, has been released. Reportedly, it was made by an arcanist director as a tribute to his old friend and fellow director, Brian Finn.
IDM's "Klein Blue" computer lost its first match against the world chess champion. John Titor declined to comment on the outcome.
When arcane scholars added Pluto to their theoretical system of astrology, one astrologist complained its energy didn't match any known planet's profile. Nobody really listened back then.
Over afternoon tea, Bunny Bunny and Satsuki talked about how to skillfully handle unruly guests and other topics unrelated to ... or perhaps related to their roles as waiters.

SPDM hired contractors to reinforce the school buildings, hoping to prevent "certain incidents" from occurring again. After the work was done, the teacher overseeing the project made sure the crew forgot all about it using a "safe" arcane skill.
Door showed a reflection of a Carolina parakeet in his mirror. He claimed it was the last one on Earth.
Ezra planned to coat either Lisa or Louise's clothes with glowing fungi so he could tell them apart. However, he gave up when he realized his plan required identifying a twin to work.
After ONiON characterized a Teakettler as a "drooly, yappy puppy" in a report about Ms. NewBabel's Critter Rehab Center party, Ms. NewBabel responded by mailing her a book on Critter ecology.
In 1987, a supernova called SN 1987A exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud. After receiving contact from Canadian astronomers, the LSCC assisted in observing and documenting the entire event.
Argus tried Tennant's M1917 revolver and agreed it was fast and lightweight. But at the end of the day, she still prefers her Summers 311A double-barreled shotgun.
During the 1979 total solar eclipse over North America, an American writer wrote, "I pray you will never see anything more awful in the sky." aliEn T said he totally agrees.
After "Giga Girl," Spathodea has discovered new game characters that have her totally hooked: a bipedal lizard with a flammable tail and a crawling frog carrying a mandrake on its back.
Vertin and Lucy played several slow chess games inside the Suitcase. Sonetto suspended the matches when Vertin ran out of energy.
Regulus had a dream where she was broadcasting a radio show from the dark side of the moon.
Pickles admits that Loggerhead is a great listener, but he wishes she could be more than that.
In a 1959 newspaper, Pioneer discovered that the first U.S. spacecraft to escape Earth's gravity shared his name.
The song "Happy Birthday to You" became a huge hit in 1924. This made Voyager wonder what people used to sing at birthday parties before that.
The "Saving the Ozone Layer" Conference was held in 1989. To share its message, Buddy Fairchild held several lectures for his friends in Antarctica.
After Noire showed the movie Zorro in her screening room, eye masks became the latest trend with the kids.

Scientists found rings around Jupiter in 1979. Pioneer joked that they should name the planetary ring system "Jupiteria" after a certain diviner friend of his, but Sputnik buzzed with concern that it would go against celestial naming conventions.
The year 1952 saw the first successful use of a mechanical heart built without any arcane power.
Hans Christian Ørsted, who discovered that electricity could create magnetism, died in 1851. By then, the age of electromagnetism was already well underway.
Fun fact: the more chickens people keep in an area, the less often Ms. Kimberly seems to show up there.

A new lunar edition of the "Special Cuisine" cookbook series has been released, featuring must-reads like How to Bake Moon Dirt and How to Safely Harvest Water from Moon Ice for space agencies everywhere.
Argus tried Sentinel's rifle, "The Nameless," and agreed it was incredibly accurate and deadly. But at the end of the day, she still prefers her Summers 311A double-barreled shotgun.
Recoleta writes so much every day that she suffers from severe semantic satiation.
Beryl predicted that the text printed on today's calendar would be this exact sentence.
Tennant made sure to avoid Brume all throughout World Consumer Rights Day.
The space age officially began in 1926 with the launch of the first liquid-fueled rocket.
Bunny Bunny decided to catch the nightly kitchen raider by using Ezra's glowing fungi.
Inside a simulation chamber, Kiperina practiced the same movements made during humanity's first spacewalk.
Since the inception of patent law in 1474, no arcanist has been granted more invention patents than X.
A group of Critters converted Dust into fuel to propel their hot-air balloon around the world, but it took a big chunk of their food supply to do it.
On the International Day of Forests, Druvis III submitted her survey and protection report about the forests of the Wilderness.
On World Water Day, Vila submitted her survey and protection report about the waters of the Wilderness.
Spathodea looked it up and found there's no World Fire Day. Good thing she's not great at writing those survey and protection reports anyway.
John Titor has found the best way to fix an old computer: call Moldir.
With no adults around, the kids huddle around a jar of fireflies at night and listen to Lopera's stories.
Sonetto had to explain to everyone that there was no siege mission, and Bunny Bunny had only borrowed Marsha's trench raider club to crack open some giant nuts.
Corvus set up a railway in the Wilderness. Most of its passengers are Critters.
Oliver Fog heard there are other big-hat wearers out there who are just as serious about clocking out on time as he is.
After asking Rubuska to shape her shadows into snakes, Kanjira wonders if they can tie themselves in knots. It turns out they can't.
Back in 1971, a coffee shop with a pureblood mermaid logo opened in Seattle. It grew into one of the world's biggest coffee chains.
When the Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889, it wasn't originally meant to shoot electricity.

The Weeping River
What is it, Sabina? Drink some water first. Take your time.
Commander Ivan
I can't. Commander, you might throw me down the well for what I'm about to say, but please—give us the order to arrest those rotten merchants. They must be punished!
Sternova
This is unlike you. Weren't you the one who told the quartermaster to "keep the well clean because you'll drink from it again"?

But I have to do something—those lying bastards are running the markets into the ground. Banknotes are nothing more than worthless scraps now. You need solid gold just to buy a bucket of moldy, rotten potatoes. It's outrageous!
Hoarding goods and profiteering from the war are nothing new. The prices here have been sky-high for ages.
A small pouch of salt now costs as much as a quartermaster's monthly wage. Do you really expect us to stand by and do nothing?
The Golden Famine is still spreading. The flour mill shut down after its workers enlisted. Life in Bereggrad keeps getting harder ...
I understand. I'll speak with Fyodor Petrovich. We can't let these parasites bleed the city dry.
Commander, you have much more to discuss with him than that.

The other day, an old man approached our soldiers with a gun, hoping to trade it for food. They agreed. Now the women, children, and elderly are gathering outside the camp, attempting to barter for rations.
I heard. Those belongings and weapons were bought with their relatives' lives. Winter is approaching, yet they've brought everything they own. They're desperate.
That's what I thought too, so I didn't order the guard company to forcibly disperse them. But there are opportunists in the crowd, using this chance to loot the locals.
Have you identified them?
Yes. They aren't bandits or infiltrators, but refugees—the stronger ones among them.
... Set up barriers outside headquarters. Post guards. Begin screening and control measures. This cannot continue.
Yes, sir! Then ... what about the women, children, and elderly?
Screen them out and get them settled. Provide as many rations as possible. I won't have these poor people getting caught in the conflict.
M-Marsha, can you hear me? We need to get her to a hospital now—
We are in a hospital! You—don't just stand there, take the children to safety. The rest of you, find a doctor!
Ptolemy
She's lost too much blood. I need some bandages ... Damn it! If I'd come along, then—
—Then we'd have two casualties on our hands!
What would Marsha do in this situation? Calm down, Merel. Think—what would Marsha do ...
Are you done? She's bleeding out! What do we do without any goddamn bandages?!
... I've got it! We can make a tourniquet with what we have ... Tear these rags into strips first ...
... Yes, like that. Wrap it tightly above the wound ... Tie a slipknot. Where's that rubber tube? Secure it ...
But she's still bleeding. Are you sure we're not killing her? ... Is that a doctor? The doctor's here! She's saved!
... Morphine? That was me. I gave her one shot ... or maybe two ... What? I shouldn't have? That's how we do it on the battlefield!
Please ... Quiet down for a moment ...
Marsha, you're awake! You're alive!
Maybe not for long. Doctor—the critical wound is in the upper left abdomen, about one-third up. Roughly half a finger deep. Gunshot wound. Please stop the bleeding there first ...
... And please use anesthesia during surgery. Pay special attention to suture tension in the tendons and protect the nerve endings. I still need to return to the front.
Have our fallen soldiers been given proper burials?
Yes. Each company held funerals with family farewells and rifle salutes, as you instructed. Nothing grand, but they can rest in peace now.
And those little росто́чки following the veterans around for bread—how did you handle them? Were they all sent away?
... I need to report a more difficult matter, Commander. During our screening we found that if we gather all the child soldiers, they could form three cavalry companies.
Our old soldiers protected them well. Emery died taking bullets for the kids in his squad. A heroic death ...
I knew Emery. He was the quartermaster in Murrey's company, wasn't he? I pinned medals on him three times—
Captain Murrey also fell in the last battle.
Commander, should we discharge all the underage soldiers? If we send them home, they might live longer.
For them—and for all the Emerys in our army—that may be the best choice. But with the Golden Famine here, does anyone have a home to return to?
You're right. Many folks along the Don have already ...
Where are the children Emery protected? I'd like to speak with them.
They're rallying other new recruits to petition to stay. They say they want to stay in the cavalry—to avenge the veterans.
... Very well. Let them stay—all these little росто́чки. If they want to help the cavalry, transfer them to logistics. They can care for the warhorses.
Thank you, Commander. I mean ... understood. I'll ensure strict supervision.
As for revenge—as long as these old horses are still around, the foals can stay out of it.
Yermolai, wait ... About that tracking serum thing—you were joking, right?
Hey, Merel. You're two hours later than yesterday. Maybe it's you who should be using a tracking serum on me, eh?
Yermolai
I get it. There's no such thing as a tracking serum, is there?
Want a drink? I hear the kitchen just received some fine bottles ...
My dear Hound, this really matters to me! I'm begging you—
... Creius? What a coincidence—you're here too!
C-Captain! My written apology is on your desk, and—
Yermolai, you tricked me again! Wait!
I had to sit through three meetings in a row this morning. My head's spinning—if you follow me again, I'll drag you straight to Creius.
W-What? Don't ...
If you ask me, we should've left you on the steppe to fend for yourself. Why did Creius insist on dragging you back for an injection?
So the tracking serum ... actually exists? I'm really getting injected?
That's right. You're getting a shot—one your beloved captain stole—ahem—took from some lab. Satisfied?
Creius ... stole it ... from a lab?
I never said that. Wake up, Blackbird. Your time's running out—I'm leaving!

Ah, we meet again—though it isn't much of a surprise.
Your move from the Western Front to the eastern one is utterly predictable.
Running around like a lost chick, following after her mother hen—or really anything big enough to grab your attention.
Will you ever learn to stand on your own? When will you grow up?
When I find her.#She's more than just a mother.
And then what? Watch her disappear again?
You're not an idiot, so why do you keep making the same mistakes?
You aren't the type to find joy in running on a treadmill, are you?
Then again—maybe you are that type after all, at least when it comes to chasing fashion.
Is the concept of family so strange to you?
What's that supposed to mean? Of course I understand family. I know what "love" is!
She attended to your every need when you were still wet behind the wings. You depended on her, clung to her—because your very survival demanded it.
Then one day, she was gone from your life. You had to fly on your own, do your own chores. You wept over the "good old days" of comfort and being cared for—oh, poor birdie.
But the truth is, that care and affection were nothing more than her way of feeding a sick obsession with control. That's what "love" is—shallow as a birdbath!
I was "loved" once. I "loved" others, too. I've experienced it firsthand, and I understand it as well as anyone!
She's key to saving the world—that's what you're saying? I'm tired of it.
Tired of sick jokes like this, with self-important ideologues bragging about securing a bright future for everyone.
You hear any cheers or laughter? Nope—because everyone who believed in their causes already died fighting for them.
If you ask me, we should hang some of those "big shots" in public. It wouldn't bring peace, of course, but maybe the rest of us would feel a little relief ...
Come, take a seat. I've set your favorite chair facing east.
The view's better that way, not to mention that the river helps wash away the stench of corpses.
Seems you've got some iron beneath that calm surface.
Not everyone would sleep so soundly in a stranger's house.
Honestly, you could've just made yourself at home and stayed the night. When I take out the trash later, I'll be sure to toss you out along with it.
I had a dream.#Did I miss dinner?
Oh, spare me the details!
I'm sure it was full of enviable warmth and radiance—just enough to scorch my miserable, frozen heart.
Whatever you saw or did in that dream, do yourself a favor and let it go.
You did—and I owe you my thanks.
Your sleep talking added a bit of flavor to my otherwise bland meal.
I haven't had such an appealing appetizer in a long time.
What about my meal?
The soup's gone cold. That ship's sailed.
You may not like the reality served on your silver platter—no one does—but you'll have to swallow it.
Blame this mess on the black robes if you want; those cowards keep trying to drag the world back to their "good old days."
And the white robes preaching the future? No less clowns for their taste in uniforms—falling off their high horses again and again, brought down by their own arrogance.
Who would have thought? The whole universe turned into one circus starring two troupes of fools.
Why didn't that blind woman just let the world burn back then? It wouldn't have been worse than these chaotic times. And who asked her to play the martyr, anyway?
If you're lucky enough to find her, take her home—and make sure she stays there, quietly, for everyone's sake.
Give me a minute; I'll go deal with the intruder.
Walking into my home with blood-soaked boots! Tsk. Such insolence. Does he think sending people to die makes him special?
He'll pay for this in blood!
Just have him change shoes.#Please calm yourself!
That's nowhere near enough. He'll have to scrub every bloodstain off the floor.
I don't want to hear any excuses. This whole mess is his own fault.
I AM calm. He brought the blood here, so he'll pay by cleaning up every drop.
I won't even lend him a rag—he can use that fancy coat of his for all I care.
So he claims those "big shots" forced him to stain his hands, huh? How convenient.
And this plan to "restore everything to how it was"? Utterly foolish.
But the fact that he followed it to the letter makes him no different from the ones who devised it.
To realize their "grand vision," those so-called realists kept piling weight on one side of the scale ...
Sacrificing one innocent life after another just so someone could remember a name that wasn't hers anymore. Absurd.
I have one thing to say to those arrogant megalomaniacs wanting to play gods: anyone who has forgotten their own name is as good as dead—and forcing them to wear it again won't change a thing.
What happened has happened. Those bloody footprints can never truly be erased.

A Conversation Among the Big Shots

Inside a Foundation office, the sound of a ringing communicator interrupts a briefing.
    Irinei glances at the device—a direct line to Zeno headquarters. He nods, signaling the committee member to wrap up mid-report. Once the door closes, he picks up.
    "Somme here. According to Ivan's report, the cavalry has been harassed by bandits for weeks."
    "Oh? Are these bandits connected to the Manus?"
    "No evidence of that. More like a mix of local warlords and scattered gangs. Though a couple of the rapidly growing factions seem suspicious."
    "Have your people maintain surveillance. Contact the Foundation the moment anything develops—we'll send reinforcements."
    Irinei is rarely this cooperative, but Somme knows he can't stake the entire steppe's fate on so-called "reinforcements."
    "No need. Ivan has enough manpower."
    "Assuming the Cavalry Corps can be fully trusted—I looked into Commander Ivan. He was a trusted subordinate to that former admiral. Plus, I heard they're both from the Don River region ..."
    "I will handle him." Somme firmly cuts off his attempt at political maneuvering.
    "I hope you understand that the Don River region is a critical component of the Foundation's strategy. To ensure downstream stability and the safety of our new recruits, supporting the Cavalry Corps is our top priority." The leader of the Hawks leaves no room for argument.
    "Save it. Since 1999, I've dealt with more politicians like you than I've smoked cigarettes. The Don is just a crack in the dam. What really matters is the line of battle along the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea, right?"
    "Stay in touch, Admiral."
    After the call ends, Irinei straightens in his chair, drumming his fingers against the desk.
    He begins to ponder: could this small "crack" pose a risk of total collapse?
A Poem Written on a Riverside Tree Trunk

Weeping Wheat

Glittering golden plains
A gentle breeze passes, yet no grain dances
The earth is like a misunderstood mother
Again and again
Reaching out her withered hands

I see sunlight fall on the fields
The wheat stands quiet and clean, almost cruel
O weeping wheat!
May you bear silent fruit, enough to sustain.
Even if only enough to fill a child's smile

—Anonymous poet, wandering along the Don
A Tea-Scented Letter

Dear Vertin,
    I hope this letter finds you well.
    I'm sorry I won't able to see you off—things have piled up due to factional disputes within the Foundation. We live in such chaos that even an organization as self-professedly rational as the Foundation cannot avoid being swept into the political whirlpool. I wish you safe travels to the Eastern Front.
    I've enclosed a copy of Commander Ivan Ivanovich Burakov's file. You're about to enter the jurisdiction of the Zeno Cavalry Corps. Ivan and Igor have known each other since childhood. Both come from an old village downstream of the Don, yet fate drove them apart along the same muddy roads. They once commanded two separate units within Zeno, nominally independent but with an unspoken understanding that lingered between them.
    Commander Ivan is difficult to gauge. According to the records, he's plainspoken and awkward in social settings, which has earned him Admiral Somme's high praise as a "loyal and trustworthy" man.
    However, I must caution you: don't place complete trust in him. Hearts rust in wartime, especially those of soldiers who've endured betrayal and hard choices. Moreover, the bond between Ivan and Igor may pose hidden risks. In times like these, you'll have to weigh trust and suspicion for yourself.
    Winter is coming to the Don. The damp cold settles heavily over riverside cities this time of year. Along with the file, I've included several packets of ginger tea. Steep it in hot water and drink—it helps ward off the chill.
    Stay in touch if you can.
    Safe travels.

Ms. Galina's Wartime Recipes

Rye Bread Aged flour, wheat husks, potato skins, a little salt. Dry and grind the potato skins, then mix them with the wheat husks into the aged flour. Add warm water and knead it into a dough, then bake beside the stove ashes. The Golden Famine leaves us short on oil and grain, so there's no oil for the bread. The baked loaf comes out hard and bitter, but at least it fills the stomach. Ivan loves smearing chilli paste on top—he says he's eaten it this way since childhood! I've made a note to prepare extra for him next time. Smoked Fish River carp, elm twigs, one old newspaper. Clean the fish, salt it, then smoke it with elm twigs and newspaper until the skin turns black and dry. The smell carries three houses down, but don't be greedy. Save the fish oil—freeze it for soup. Grass Roots Soup Ingredients: Wild grass roots, nettles, half a potato, a pinch of chili. Instructions: Boil the roots until soft, add chili, stove ash, and salted grass seeds to mimic borscht. The recipe came from a young man I met by the riverside wheat field. He claimed to be a nameless wandering poet. *Missing Ingredients: Sour cream, carrots, and onions. Can't make proper borscht. Grass roots have been dug out nearly everywhere. I can only forage along the ditches now. Jam from Neighbor Valia Note: They hid two jars of real apple jam before the famine hit, and gave me one ... I've tucked it on the top shelf of the cupboard, wrapped in old cloth so the rats won't smell it. Her husband lost an entire wheat field's harvest ... May the Mother Earth bless this kind couple. *I've told Ivan to stop bringing food home. The people at the front have it harder than we do. Besides, in the face of disaster, soldiers and civilians must be treated equally! Even with his position, I won't allow our family any special treatment.

The Lost Diary of a Captive

[An old diary with black, viscous stains smeared across its cover. The corners are torn and dog-eared. It seems the owner abandoned it recently.] November 11 Every night since my capture, I've heard terrifying, fragmented whispers coming from outside ... and screams—not just one or two people, but many, shrieking and wailing in pain. I can also smell something burning and rotting. Damn it, are those Manus dogs burning corpses? Or performing some twisted ritual? ... November XX I've lost track of the date. Time and life hold no meaning in this godforsaken place. I once saved lives as a doctor ... now, they've used my medical instruments to brutally murder Boyaryshkin, Artyom, and Malyekhov right in front of me. I don't care anymore. If they're going to come for me eventually, they might as well hurry and end it now. ... November XX I don't know how to write this. I actually survived that nightmare—which feels like a curse in itself. We were herded onto an empty clearing where a koldunya in black robes was chanting a song. I could barely make out the words: "... Inculcator of Arcanum, let me manifest decay anew." She pulled away the shroud covering the corpse. As the black mist dissipated, a broken body lay before us. She handed me my old scalpel: "Dissect it." I looked down at the remains exposed to the air. Male, early twenties. Mottled, wrinkled skin. Ribs collapsed and fractured. I didn't know what I was doing—fear made me forget everything I once believed. Standing beside her, I raised the blade and started cutting. The scraping of bone was monotonous, but I freed that soul from its mortal prison. When I lowered the knife, I realized we were surrounded by a black fog reeking of death. All the other captives had died, their faces twisted in agony. The koldunya seized my filthy hand and laughed: "Thank you, Charon! You helped me unravel death and command it, master Death, and aid its power!" ... November XX Boyaryshkin, Artyom, Malyekhov—they came for me! I didn't mean to! I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry ... Valley, Outside the Ancient City of Ai-Khanoum
Along the riverbank, young riders grip their reins as they make their way back toward the village garrison.
At the head of the column rides the [Lieutenant] on her red-brown [Akhal-Teke], and behind her the slanting sun sweeps westward, hanging alone at the edge of the earth.
Snow peaks rise with solemn majesty, catching the late-fall afterglow before casting their shadows downward. The horsemen ride through this ancient dusk, winding their way back toward the garrison.
Their luck has run thin today. Several soldiers lost their way, and the rendezvous has been set an hour late to give them time to rejoin the column.
Out of consideration for her new recruits—young soldiers newly arrived to this unfamiliar land—she holds out just a little longer.
And her fortunes turn. As Lieutenant Moldir prepares to send riders out to search, her stragglers finally appear on the hillside, overdue but unharmed.
"Pick it up. We need to be back before nightfall."
"Is everyone accounted for?"
She lifts the reins, and her horse rises before breaking into a few quick strides, circling back along the flank of the column toward the rear.
"Six, seven, eight ..."
She counts each rider, making certain each man and mount match. No soldier left behind, and no horse allowed to lose its way home.
"Fyodor, what are you carrying in those side pouches?"
She brings her horse to a halt beside one of the soldiers, turns the mount, and rides in step with the young soldier, pointing to the crude burlap pouches hanging from his saddle.
Fyodor
"Picked up a few fine catches this afternoon. Nothing beats hunting at this time of the year!"
The soldier loosens the pouches and proudly shows his treasures to his commanding officer.
"Be prepared. We could be sent to the front anytime."
"Haha, yeah! I'm itching to go!"
The young soldier laughs, glancing back at his comrades.
"We've been waiting for it! This is how all young men should live: on horseback, rifle in hand, carving out glorious legends on the battlefield."
Soldiers
"Aye! Aye!"
His headstrong words earn a cheer from the others.
"Just watch! We'll pick off the enemy one by one, like hunting rabbits."
"With that rifle? Hmm, seems you're a decent enough shot."
"Naturally! No one brings in more game than I do! Every shot bags a kill with me. I never miss!"
The lieutenant presses into her stirrup, draws close to Fyodor, then snatches the rifle slung over his shoulder.
"We didn't have any shooting drills today. I did not give you permission to fire your weapon."
With that, she changes her tone, confiscates the rifle, and quickly pulls back onto her own mount.
"Order must be maintained, Fyodor. If you don't know when to pull the trigger, you will hand the gun over to me."
"I don't want this to happen again."
She raises her voice, issuing the order to everyone in the line.
"Drop whatever you've hunted. All of you."
"Yes, ma'am."
With the confiscated rifle in hand, she urges her horse forward, returns to the head of the column, and turns to deliver her command.
"I understand your enthusiasm, but orders come before everything. Discipline above all else."
"Right. Now get rid of anything you weren't carrying when you left camp."
As the last word leaves her mouth, she nudges her boot against her horse's flank. The mount catches the signal at once, its pace quickening until it surges into a gallop.
She grips the reins with both hands and leans forward, rising and falling like a wave in time with the Akhal-Teke's gallop.
"Keep up!"
Riding at the front, the lieutenant leans into the wind and glances back. The riders who had been idling along the river earlier are now picking up speed to keep pace with her.

Among them are both the so-called "rebels" withdrawn from Antarctica and the young recruits the Admiral has gathered since returning to this era. Few of the former remain, while the latter, like Fyodor, make up the bulk of the column.
Hooves hammer the earth, their numbers causing the earth to tremble around them, holding a tight formation as they approach the garrison.
The lieutenant rides a good seven or eight lengths ahead, watching the line behind her as she scolds herself beneath her breath.
"Give them a little more time. We'll make them soldiers soon enough."
A stray wave of nostalgia rises up in her chest. Old memories drift around her like ghosts. She closes her eyes to empty her thoughts and fall into rhythm with the horse beneath her.
For a girl born deep on the inland steppes of Asia, all of this comes easy. With so much of her time wrapped up in military duties and camp chores, the chance to ride feels like a long-awaited rest.
It's a fleeting and precious rest, letting her soul run free in the rush of the evening wind.
"Make the most of it, boys."
"Last one back to camp is on stable duty with Fyodor."

She calls out the command, and somewhere behind her a loud wail rises, chased by bursts of laughter. The horses keep their pace, the sun falling lower as the group nears the village where they're stationed.
Military Camp, Outside the Ancient City of Ai-Khanoum
Their camp sits in a riverside village beyond the ancient city of Ai-Khanoum, not far from the ruins where her unit has set up camp.
By the time the lieutenant returns with her riders, the sun has only just dipped behind the peak. For the locals, that means night has already fallen.
"Make sure he's fed."
She is the first to step down from the stirrup, offering a long and reassuring pat to the Akhal-Teke that has carried her all day. After a gentle reminder, she hands the reins to the stable boy.

Soon enough her men dismount and gather around her, chatting idly over the day's training and their detour.
Still talking and laughing, she makes her way toward the fire-lit courtyard.
"Is that so? Go have Doctor Yelena take a look. If you can still walk, jump, and carry things, it probably isn't anything serious."
She lifts the new recruit's sleeve, revealing the mark left from his fall off the horse earlier in the day.
"Nothing serious. At your age, I hit the ground far worse and far more often."
With that, she pats the young man on the shoulder and sends them all off, walking alone toward a courtyard fenced in by earthen walls.
The fire represents the villagers' welcome, a sign of light and good intent. People gather around it, passing tea, dried fruit, and warm smiles.
Here, all is calm and quiet, far from war and turmoil. The lieutenant approaches the village elder, and the aging man meets her with a grin.
Old Man
"Drink, traveler from afar. May the flame light your path."
"Thank you."
The lieutenant takes the bowl of milk wine in both hands and finishes it with a single gulp.
She recognizes the flavor: a taste of her childhood, long before she donned a soldier's uniform. In the safety of her grandmother's home, a life that was simple and carefree.

Now, after leaving the frozen wastes of Antarctica and returning to an unfamiliar age, she has taken on a new assignment: travelling to the far eastern highlands and river valleys to take command of a newly reformed unit, with orders to make them ready for the battles ahead.
"We'll be staying here for a few days, sir. Thank you for taking us in."
She takes a seat beneath the thick trunk of a desert poplar, her eyes lingering on the bonfire burning nearby.

The blaze gives off a faint warmth even at this distance. In the courtyard beyond, troops and the ever-hospitable villagers mingle and joke as they pass around milk wine, salted lamb, and thick, stuffed samsa pastries.
The fire's light creates a tiny patch of life in the still darkness, an island of peace in this age of war.
"We welcome our guests, as we always have. But tell me, what name should I give my people when they ask who you are?"
An admiral's adjutant.#A Zeno officer.
Your decision changes what is yet to come.
"We've come from further north. My father commands a unit there in the Don River region."
Father.
"Ah, a Hetman."
As the elder speaks the title, he raises his pipe and pulls in a deep breath. Firelight spills across his lined, weathered face, tracing every crease and old scar.
"Yes. A Hetman, and a respected one. That's a fair way of putting it."
"I'm an officer from the Zeno Arms Academy."

The lie curdles on her tongue. But then she reminds herself that, though she may not bear the title, her life is nonetheless bound to Zeno through her past, her adoptive father, and the sisters and brothers she grew up with.
"Academy?"
There is a touch of doubt in his hoarse voice. The firelight paints his white beard with streaks of burning red.
"It's where soldiers like me are trained."
"My ancestors were fighters too. They came from far away across the western sea and made their home here."
"Yes. I know. That is why I've come here."
"I seek your support, elder."
She states her purpose plainly: to recruit more soldiers for her father's army and to strengthen their influence in the remote regions along their rear flank.
The old man's eyes narrow, revealing a depth of wisdom behind his gaze.
"And what would you give us in return, officer?"
"Protection."
She names her terms with a steady, unguarded honesty.
Her father stationed her here so she could drum up support for the front lines and so she could win over every force that has not yet chosen to oppose them.
Stone by stone, a citadel rises. Small gains become towering strength. The lieutenant understands this well. If the battle roars in the west, then she rides east to gather allies.
"Our troops in Ai-Khanoum are more than enough to maintain peace in this region."
Peace. Simple, direct, and powerful.
The old man holds a long silence, opening his shaking right hand as though laying the village before his far-traveled guest.

This particular village has been built around a medieval citadel, which climbs up the mountainside, pressed tight against the slope, overlooking the pass along the river moving east-to-west. It's a perfect chokepoint.

"When my ancestors mounted their horses and drew their curved blades, they were warriors. When they dismounted and donned their robes, they were merchants. From east to west, west to east, this is how we have lived for twenty-odd centuries."
"We are friends to all who meet us."
As he speaks, the old man waves someone over. A girl in her early teens comes at his gesture, her face glowing in the firelight like an unripe little orange.
"This is my last remaining granddaughter. Her brothers answered the call from the north and have gone far from here."
"I'm Lieutenant Moldir; I'm very pleased to meet you."
The lieutenant rises and, following the local custom, touches her right cheek to the girl's, then her left, in a gesture of goodwill.
The girl nods respectfully as she steps to her elder's side.
"If you wish, I will ready my finest horse for her and allow her to join you as one of your warriors."
"No, you just said she was your last granddaughter."
The lieutenant's composure wavers for a moment.
"I did not expect you to refuse another woman in your company."
The old man looks at the lieutenant with a long, knowing gaze.
"No, that isn't what I meant. I'm hoping to find more fighters of the right age here."
"Everyone in this village can trace their blood back to the same heroic ancestors. Her father and brothers have never brought shame upon us."
The old man takes his granddaughter by the hand.
"You're just as good as those rowdy boys, aren't you?"
The young girl offers a silent nod.
"Ma'am, please take her along. Look after her, and let her fight at your side like a hawk."
Faced with the sudden request, the lieutenant pauses, searching for a reply.
The girl's eyes are like polished jade, green as the grass in spring.
The lieutenant can't help thinking the girl belongs tending to a pasture, not fighting on a battlefield.
"Perhaps the life she has now would suit her better."
"Why would you ...?"
She looks toward the girl, and in this unfamiliar young face, she catches a fleeting glimpse of someone she once knew.
Pastures and herds—they're her own childhood and the peaceful life that is all this mere child knows. She should be holding a docile lamb, not lifting a rifle.
"I don't have many days left."
The old man strokes his beard. Age has worn him down. He can no longer even draw a bowstring; the vigor of his youth eroded like a wind-etched stone.
He turns back to the guest beside him.

The bonfire casts shadows of the village along the mountainside. In its glow, they seem to honor the ancient gods they've served for ages—light, flame, and the good that stands against its eternal enemy.
The trade roads have been cut off for years now, and no caravan bells have echoed through the valley for generations.
The fortress built into the cliffside is a crumbling ruin, hewn like a sandcastle carved from red stone, slowly slipping out of time's remembrance.
"Peace."
"This is something we are well acquainted with."
He braces himself on his lapis lazuli cane and takes a step forward.
"But I also know the price of peace."
"That is why they listen to me and why they will listen to those who come after me."
The old man answers, his voice never rising above an even tone, like the wind softly whipping through the mountains.
"The support you ask for will be yours."
"But first, I would like to know more about you, our visitors from far away."
"The flames reveal all. Come. Let us speak by their light."
A few soldiers, their caps and jackets off, walk toward them. When they see the village elder shaking hands with their commanding officer, their smiles vanish.
Young Officer
"Pardon me. I'm not interrupting, am I?"
"What is it?"
"It's nothing, really. We just wanted to ..."
The young men glance at one another, rubbing the backs of their necks, clearly unsure of how to proceed.
"Wanted to ...?"
"We just wanted to ask if you wanted to dance with us."
It's an earnest, friendly invitation from the boys who, just earlier, were over by the fire dancing arm-in-arm with the villagers.
"Oh. So that's what this is about."
The lieutenant lets out a quiet laugh, covering her mouth before giving a small wave of her hand.
"We still have matters to discuss. I'll join you all later."
"O-Okay. But actually, I have one more question. Just a quick one!"
"Speak."
"A girl over there just asked if I had the guts to kiss her, and I ... I don't know what to do."
His face goes beet red as he blurts out the words. She looks at him and laughs. He is her family and also an ace pilot who earned his merits in Antarctica.
"Where has your courage gone, soldier? You would fly into the jaws of death but run from the lips of a pretty girl? Do you need my permission? Go on then; don't keep her waiting."
"Y-Yes, ma'am!"
After giving a comically awkward salute, the soldiers trot off toward the crowd.
She lets her smile fade, then turns to walk after the old man, heading toward the fire and coming to a stop beside the stacked logs.
On the way over, the old man hands her an almond.
"You're probably not used to flavors this bitter, but we're quite fond of them here."
The lieutenant holds the almond between her fingers and eats it. The flavor is sharper than she expected, upturning her face into a scowl before she manages to swallow it.
"You're right about that."
"Bitterness clears the mind. Before the fire, we speak no lies."
"A deeper understanding between us will serve our future cooperation well."
When they reach the bonfire, the old man slips on a white cloth mask as if fearing his aging breath would profane their sacred flame.
The lieutenant approaches the flame with a touch of hesitation, the rich, stark smell of smoke lingering on her nose and lips.
"Step closer. Do not fear it. The flames will reveal the truth in your heart."
"What do you see?"
A courtyard in the pouring rain and the barrel of a gun.#A girl on horseback, riding across the grasslands.
"I raised a weapon against my own family."
"I fired at her in the pouring rain."
"I ... I abandoned her."
The memories flickering in the flames make her throat tighten.
"You must have had no choice. Something must have forced your hand."
"No. I knew exactly what I was doing."
"Dusk and a band of horses. They race across the grasslands that seem to stretch on forever, and a girl rides with them."
"I know that young rider. She was always like that, riding beyond the horizon, stopping only when her horse chose to rest, lifting her face to stare at the stars above."
"She wanted to become a scientist, just like her mother."
But fate had other ideas.
"In the end, she picked up a gun."
Her hand moves to her sidearm before she even thinks about it. It's a gesture long since ingrained in her.
"We are nothing more than driftwood carried on the current."
"You're right."
"I see my past."
"Everything that made me who I am."
The lieutenant drifts back into her memories, slowly tracing her way through the past.
Seizing the moment, she begins telling the old man a story about a girl she knows better than anyone, a girl no one else could ever know as well.
"When I was sixteen, I received two pieces of paper."
Red and orange firelight washes over her face, while outside its glow, people laugh and dance, fluttering through the shadows like butterflies beating their wings toward another world.
"The first told me that my parents were gone. The second that I had a new father."
The lieutenant murmurs the words to herself by the fire.
"No one ever asked what I thought, and back then, not one choice in my life was mine to make."
She makes herself a little space by the fire and sits, left leg relaxed and bent, hands resting at her sides, vision locked on the burning embers.
The old man stands beside her, listening in silence.
"I was his first child."
"No other soldier has remained at his side as long as I have."
"Some he took in after me, and some fought beside him long before I arrived, but few have made it all the way to now."
"That day, the Admiral, my adoptive father, took me to the Hall of Merit at headquarters."
She picks up a dry twig and stirs the fire with it.
Hall of Merit, Zeno Arms Academy
"Solemn. Silent. They call it a memorial hall, a place that houses the deeds of the fallen."
"Whether soldier or commander, the fallen all have a place there."
"Cold metal, stone, and light."
A far cry from the warm, living fire before her.
"I found my mother's and father's names there. My biological father."
"They sacrificed their lives for a worthy cause."
"Heroes and martyrs both."
"And I ..."
She pauses, waiting for the words to come.
"I am the child of martyrs, yet I find myself on a path I never could have dreamed of."
A wry smile crosses her face, an acknowledgment of fate's cruel irony.
"Seeing their portraits, I felt a strange calm, hoping that one day I, too, could be there beside them."
"Unfortunately, that hope became reality."
"Why do you say 'unfortunately'?"
The old man doesn't look at her; he keeps his eyes steady on the flame, his expression neutral.
"I've been told that my adoptive father's name and mine are now etched into that hall."
She answers with a bitter smile.
"I can't say if it was meant as a joke or an insult, but I know that I'll never have the chance to see it with my own eyes."
"Will our past honors be preserved? Will I bring shame to my parents' legacy?"
"They called us traitors."
She shakes her head, looking at the old man, but he remains motionless.
He repeats his earlier words; the crackling firelight dances over his face.
"This is your story."
"It's part of my story."
"Fate has treated me well. It took one family from me, then gave me another, like those two letters."
"The Admiral took in other orphans like me, bringing them under his command."
"At the arms academy, or at his camp."
"As his daughter, I was given authority over the youngest adoptees."
"In better times, they should have still been in their parents' arms, not fighting in some cold barren field being corralled and commanded to obey."
"My granddaughter was the same way when she was a child."
"A wild little foal, always so stubborn and fierce."
"I thought she’d be as gentle as she looks."
She laughs softly and bitterly before she returns to the topic.
"Not long after, my father brought a few boys to join us. They were close, as close as cubs raised in the same den."
"But years passed, and the young cubs fell until only Ptolemy was left. War took his brothers, and along with them, an eye."
"He became cold and cruel after that, twisted by one mission after another."
"Ten set out, and only three returned."
"If he were numb to it all, he'd have learned to disregard death, to the point where his own life would mean nothing, and he'd become a fugitive."
"And if he wasn't, every one of their deaths turned that anger further inward, and each turn made him that much more ruthless."
"And I can't blame him. Because I know what molded him."
"Even so, I know his sins cannot be washed away."
The words come out calm without condemnation.
"But you still see him as your family?"
"Family? Always, the same as these boys."
The lieutenant tilts her head with a half-hearted smile as she gestures toward the other side of the fire.
A few of the soldiers spot their sister and wave from afar, holding half a roasted lamb leg.
"I just hope that this time they'll get to live, not just survive."
"But they're hungry for battle; many of them think it will be like hunting rabbits on the steppe."
"But in war, the hunters and the hunted are one and the same."
"All they know of death and sacrifice comes from stories or propaganda."
A trace of disgust flickers across her face.
"I hope that it will all be as easy as they think—winning honor and glory."
She sighs.
Honor. Glory.
The words glimmer like two medals soaked in blood.
"So, you see these soldiers as your family."
"Yes. They are all my brothers. I also have a sister."
"And your sister? What kind of person did she turn out to be?"
"She's still the same stubborn little girl."
"Luckier than Ptolemy."
Two emotions cross her face and battle beneath the surface: nostalgia and regret.
"The last time I saw her, we had raised our guns toward one another."
"She said goodbye with a bullet. It was her way of returning the one I shot at her in the rain."
"I used to call her Pera."
"Pera. Lopera."
There wasn't any trick to the name; it was short and simple.
"First, press your lips together, then part them, and gently drop your tongue toward your chin."
"It sounds light, floral maybe, like the frail creature I saw when I met her."
"An unripe orange, fallen to the ground too soon."
"Do oranges grow around here?"
She asks the old man, who gently shakes his head.
"Right. I'd never seen an orange back home, either."
She asks herself a question, then answers it.
"Tarter than grapes, sweeter than plums."
Zeno Arms Academy
"A runaway child."
"Father brought her in, and we couldn't help but be curious about the little girl with her orange hair."
"Ptolemy sized her up with his one good eye."
"I remember the first thing he said to her: 'You're shorter than I expected.'"
She mimics her brother's tone as she speaks.
"Lopera walked right up to him, stood up on her tiptoes, and pulled him down by the collar. 'Call me short again, I dare you.'"
"And just like that we were all laughing; Ptolemy could still laugh back then. But not Father. Even then, he stood there, solid as stone."
"I could see him watching her with that cold, calculating gaze, studying her, waiting for her next move."
"I know what he must have been thinking. Most fathers would feel the same."
"Ptolemy, naturally, couldn't help but meet the challenge. He went down a list of words, 'runt, shrimp, short stuff,' as if he had them prepared. He's always had a cruel sense of humor."
"Father and I simply sat back and waited for what would happen next."
She sighs. Reliving these memories has been a welcome rest from her [Exhaustion and Mental Strain].
"She practically leaped as she yanked down on his collar; Ptolemy tumbled over her shoulder like a sack of oats."

"I can still remember that stunned look on his face, staring up at the sky, then we all turned to Father. I already knew what we would see. The same nearly imperceptible smile he gave any of us when he was pleased."
"Ptolemy was furious; he pulled her down into the mud right along with him. The training grounds were always muddy, even on sunny days. I think that was by design."
"I tried to pull them apart, yelled at them to stop, but Ptolemy had long since stopped listening to me. And Lopera ... I'm not sure she ever did."
"There was nothing I could do."
She says it with a smile.
"Eventually, I managed to grab ahold of my new sister, like grabbing an orange, and pulled her out from the muck. Ptolemy reached for her, but I stood in his way."
"I told him he needed to cool off."
"That was their first fight, certainly not the last. I'm sure those two fought more than anyone else."
"All of our siblings fought. Father encouraged it. He believed it made us tougher, more resilient. Sometimes that was true."
The old man nods, as if in agreement.
"I taught her how to hold a gun."
"I also taught her how to ride, how to match the horse's rhythm, and how to aim while on horseback."
Happy memories flood to the surface, playing out like a movie lit by the flickering flames.
"That's how things were, the good and the bad."
"But things change."
The sun has long since set, and a clear starry sky has replaced it.
The chill mountain air creeps up from the darkness, making the bonfire's heat feel all the more precious.
She shifts her gaze up from the fire to the moon. A familiar sight in an unfamiliar time.
"We come from somewhere very far away."
She tells her story.
"But no matter where we go, the moon is the same."
"When I was young, I would often sit with my grandmother and watch it as it hung above the sky."
"Later, whenever we weren't on patrol or training late, my sister and I would do the same."
"I remember once, when she was still young, she ran up to me, tugging at my sleeve, saying, 'Molly, I've got something to show you!'"
"She pulled me up from my desk and dragged me outside."
"I followed her to the courtyard, and there was that pale moon. She stood beside me, looking up at it."
The lieutenant lets her head fall back, looking up at the dark and starry sky.
"You left her."
"Yes, I did. She was free to follow her own sense of right and wrong, to choose a different path. That's who she is, and that's how it should be."
"I wonder if she still looks up in the sky and thinks of me."
She closes her eyes.
"I told her once."
"We're soldiers. Goodbye is a luxury in our profession."
"Ptolemy understood that all too well, and so did the other soldiers."
"But Lopera never seemed to take it seriously; she thought of it like a game."
She hesitates.
"It wasn't."
She casts a glance at the soldiers singing and dancing with the villagers.
"Most of them have never shot at anything that could shoot back."
"Rabbits, birds, deer, maybe a wolf or a bear."
"A hunter is not a soldier just because he can fire a rifle. No more than climbing on a horse makes you a knight."
The old man nods in firm agreement.
"You speak truly."
"To be a soldier is to be both the best and the worst of humanity."
"I still remember their names."
Her voice trails off.
After taking two deep breaths, she begins again, reciting the names as if they were a solemn vow.
"[Marshall], who was always better with a sword than a gun, [Whitewood], who took better care of his books than his rifle, and [Vasilisa], with her falcon ..."
Their names linger as ghostly wisps in the night air.
"Lopera and I were supposed to go out on a mission; it was her first opportunity to witness a battlefield firsthand."
"But just before we left, Father decided to leave the two of us behind."
I still don't understand why.#I remember how disappointed she was.
"We were still at the station, waiting for the train, when the messenger showed up with orders for us to turn back to base."
"By the time I finished reading, the train had pulled into the station. The others started getting on, one after another."
"The disappointment on her face hardened into something else."
Sadness became protest. Protest turned to rage.
"All I could do was grab her hand and tell her to follow orders."
"I didn't understand Father's reasoning, but I followed his orders."
"Just as I always have."
"I keep my opinions to myself, and I follow my orders."
"Lopera screamed in the middle of the station, demanding to know why she couldn't go to the front."
"The fall was colder than usual, and it was already snowing. I can still picture those white flakes that dotted her orange hair."
"As she yelled and protested, all the soldiers turned to look at us. So many familiar faces. I thought perhaps the message meant that the war was ending, that we weren't needed there."
"But that was the last time I saw many of those faces. Some of them I once called siblings too."
"They went to war. We went home. Those were Father's orders."
She lowers her head.
"It wasn't long after that we received the first of their remains. Lopera dug the graves herself."
"It was snowing that day too."
She feels a chill run down her spine, one that doesn't belong to the cold air around her but to that distant memory.
"Fate brought me to my father and then, one after another, brought others to our side."
"They would come and go, live and die, then more would come. Orphans created by and for war."
Exhaustion lingers in her voice.
"War forces us to grow to adapt to our conditions, to the brutality around us."
"It's not right to say 'grow'; we survive. Those that adapt survive."
She bites down on her lower lip, her brow furrowing.
"My sister has been on many missions. But I don't know if she's ever seen that side of war for herself. I never got the chance to ask. I never wanted to—"
She opens her hands.
"I hope not. I hope, in some way, she never has to adapt to the cruelties that I have: the brutal calculus of command. She's suited to what she does. She isn't meant for the front lines."
The old man pulls an almond from his sleeve and hands it to her.
The lieutenant takes it, her face scrunching involuntarily, anticipating the oncoming tartness.
"And what was it that changed you?"
"A battle that wasn't worth remembering, when I shot a man I didn't know."
A Historical Battlefield
Years ago, the Admiral brought his daughter to the battlefield.
They flew in during the final days of the war. She was still being trained as an officer.
From the window of their plane, she could see husks of concrete buildings jutting out like bones over the scarred landscape.
It was her first real taste of the battle—an assault on a fortified position.
"We secured the street. We had tanks then, large armored vehicles with cannons."
She explains for the man. Though perhaps even the notion of a motor vehicle might elude him.
"But tanks are no use in taking a building. I led the troops in; I think we had reached the third or fourth floor without opposition.
"Then I heard a voice. A man speaking in a language I didn't know. I turned to see a stranger."
"It didn't take long before he saw me too."
"I reached for my gun. He raised his."
The lieutenant taps her thumb on her chest, signaling with a small gesture.
The old man nods in understanding, his wrinkled thumb turning the lapis lazuli beads on his wrist.
"I reacted on instinct. Father's training. It was over in a single shot."
"Then, I don't know why, but I crumpled to the ground and lay there. My mind went blank."
"My comrades came running over; they thought I had been hit."
Her hand trembles on her chest. The moment replays itself in her mind.
"They told me I was crying and throwing up as they dragged me out to safety."
"All that training. All that was expected of me. Honor and glory, a martyr's death."
"But I only killed that man because I was afraid to die myself."
"I couldn't escape the look on his face as I shot him."
"For a long time after, even in training, if I heard a gunshot, I would feel sick to my stomach."
"Until one day I changed. That sickness in my stomach just went away."
"Or maybe I learned to live with it."
The old man stops twisting the beads with his fingers. The fire twinkles back at her in the bright blue reflection.
"It is a feeling all soldiers must learn to live with."
"It's getting late."
"I appreciate you listening to me, sir."
"You are my guest."
The lieutenant nods respectfully.
The music has picked up again, a familiar song that brings a wave of cheers from the nearby revelers.
Smoke rises up into the night sky before fading into the canopy of stars.
"May I ask that young lady over there if I can borrow the dombra?"
"Of course."
He raises his hands and claps. The musician, noticing the gesture, stops playing and walks over with the instrument in hand.
"The young commander wishes to perform a song for us."
The old man calls out to the people in the yard.
"Haha, please, I didn't mean to stop everything on my account."
"I suddenly feel as if I'm about to embarrass myself."
She takes the instrument, testing the sound, like reacquainting with an old friend.
Her soldiers gather around, eager to join in.
Curious villagers trail behind, edging closer to the honored guest.
"You're gonna play a song, Lieutenant?"
"That's right. I thought I might show you all that I can relax too."
She sits down with the instrument, facing the bonfire and the people waiting by it, and begins to play; her voice, initially soft, rises into a clear and bright song—a memory of her homeland.
"Oh golden summer, you've lingered too long. ♪"
"We lift our cups to the dwindling days. ♪"
As she plays, several voices join in harmony, following and stumbling over the words.
"To salute the sun as it sinks away. ♪"
"Oh golden years of youth, how fast you've gone. ♪"
"For cold winter's breath will find us in the dawn. ♪"
"Reminding us to savor our days and the warmth of the sun. ♪"
"So live and love while the night is young. ♪"
She's stood up without ever realizing it, losing herself in her song, as if she were lifted from time and space entirely.
"Alright, alright. That's enough for now."
She waves away the cheers of the crowd and promptly returns the dombra.
"It's been so long since I last played. I'd almost forgotten how ..."
She offers a self-deprecating chuckle, shaking her head as her voice fades away.
"Go on, enjoy yourselves."
At this, the crowd breaks out in laughter and then begins to follow the musician as they resume the previous melody.
As the crowd disperses, the old man approaches again.
"Do you think about her often?"
Yes, often.#Now and then, but ...
The lieutenant loses herself in thought, reflecting on the past. Until, after a long pause, she speaks.
"When she joined us, things were a lot like this. We danced, we celebrated, and I remember playing that song for them as well."
"She's always been a fighter, from the moment we met."
"There is a difference between that and a soldier."
"Just like there's a difference between us."
"She'll always be my sister, but that wildness in her ..."
"We grew apart. Maybe there was nothing that could stop us from growing apart."
"All that matters to me now are the lives of these soldiers under my command."
"The past is a river we've already crossed; tomorrow matters, yesterday does not."
"You're right."
"I suppose she was always going to grow up."
"My sister isn't the kind to feel helpless. She won't cry herself to sleep if I'm not there with her."
"She's a Zeno soldier."
The lieutenant stresses the words, her gaze firm.
"She made that choice for herself."
"We tried to force her down a path she couldn't follow."
"Sometimes, I wonder if I had just explained things to her from the beginning, if I had said the right words, would she have chosen differently?"
Her tone is wistful; it catches her off-guard to have let something so naive slip out.
"I don't know."
She shakes her head. It wasn't that she didn't know. It's that she knew there was no answer.
"She's always lived according to her own rules, her own conscience."
"And I would never take that from her."
A bitterness holds on her tongue as tart as the old man's almonds. Her sister's image feels faint and distant; she can't even recall the sound of her voice.
What comes to her mind, instead, is the thundering rattle of gunfire.
A sweltering afternoon. Thick, humid air that clings to her skin, mixing with beads of sweat.
She guides her sister's hand, telling her to aim at the target and not hesitate when pulling the trigger.
Decisive and resolute.
"Just like her dice games, she could lose every time and never regret it, no matter how badly she lost."
"Perhaps while I was away, she really grew up."
Military Camp Office, Outside the Ancient City of Ai-Khanoum
A brief message is placed on the lieutenant's desk.
November 11, 1920. Ceasefire on the Western Front.
Your forces remain stationed in Ai-Khanoum. Recruit, prepare, and await further orders.
"Their war is over."
"But mine isn't."
She opens the window, facing out toward the snow-covered mountains as they glimmer in the morning light.
From a distance, she can see her new recruits—young people from the village—leading their horses to the river after their morning patrol.
She idly twists a medal in her hand. Not a mark of battle or a reward for service.
It was one of a kind, a gift for the "World's #1 Sister."
I hope I'll see her somewhere on the Eastern Front.#I hope she isn't anywhere near the Eastern Front.
"Maybe she'll end up deployed to the Eastern Front."
"I don't know. Maybe they won't send her to the front lines again."
"But then again, who knows? Father is there, after all."
Her voice falls into a low rumble.
She stares down at the rusted medal, damaged and tarnished. She doubts it would survive any attempt to mend it.
"She'd be better off staying away from this war. In fact, I pray we never see her at all."
"Father won't show her any mercy."
She clenches the medal, the cold metal carrying a warmth that's hers and hers alone.
"She wouldn't either."
She picks up her rifle and turns to head outside. Her troops are waiting for her.
The crisp fall air fills the sky outside, clear and boundless, illuminated with the rising sun.

"I've got nothing more to say."
"They're traitors, and he's gone. I don't know who's running their little rebellion now."

"What about Moldir?"
