From El Semanario Heraldo de México

Yesterday afternoon, a foreign diplomat arrived in Mexico City. His motorcade proceeded along Bucareli Street into the city center, making a brief stop at the Zócalo. Streetcar bells echoed through the streets as vendors laid out bundles of marigolds ahead of Día de los Fieles Difuntos. The gentleman is said to be no stranger to Aztec mythology, the Sun Stone, and the origins of the festival.

Later in the day, he visited the Academia de San Carlos, where he commented briefly on the public murals that have recently drawn attention. His interest, however, extended well beyond the academy walls. At a quiet corner of La Merced Market, the guest paused before several shop windows, taking in the prints, candy skulls, and papel picado on display. Though simply crafted, each piece carried a rich emotional weight. One piece held his attention above all others—a calavera figurine engraved with satirical verse. He turned it over repeatedly, praising it without reserve, and offered no reply even as his entourage urged him onward.

No further details regarding the diplomat's remaining itinerary have been released. Nevertheless, during this festival when the dead return and the living rejoice, our distinguished visitor has proven himself far more than a passing observer. Mexico City may soon count among its guests an uncommon connoisseur of the arts.

Reported by Fitzwilliam
The City and the "City"

After the "Storm," the Vigiles Bureau returns to every "important city" following the same pattern—an unremarkable office at first, then a few Vigils, and before long, people simply grow accustomed to its presence as though it has always belonged there.

According to official records, the Vigiles Bureau exists to investigate complex cases involving arcanum. It operates independently of the government, each fulfilling its own mandate without interfering with the other's affairs, though the two maintain steady communication.

At the same time, the criminal underworld enters what the press calls the age of "modern crime." The most dangerous example of which is known as "El Automóvil Gris" or the Grey Car Gang, driving in their eponymous automobiles with matching grey attire. Their increasingly organized robberies and violence have given them a steady spot in the crime columns. Their methods have been dissected and debated at length, yet no amount of analysis softens the reality of what they are. People have begun to realize that violence and plunder are becoming more organized and more efficient. Crime is no longer a matter for the police alone—it has become a reality the whole of society can no longer afford to ignore.

Of course, the Grey Car Gang alone is not enough to shake the order of an entire city. The local police know the limits of their authority, and the Vigiles Bureau understands how to avoid raising questions outside its jurisdiction. The underworld and the authorities share the same map—they simply disagree on how to read it.

This seemingly harmonious coexistence does not eliminate conflict, only confines it. Police, Vigils, and grey cars pass through the same streets, fully aware of one another. They all understand the same unspoken truth—when the sun rises, the streets return to normal. Everything dissolves into the daylight, folding back into the city's shadow.
The Muralism Movement, Part I

In early twentieth-century Mexico, no art form is more woven into everyday life than the art of the mural. Too large for any private collection, they occupy stairwells, courtyards, and corridors. It is for this reason that the muralism movement sparks continuous debate—about art itself, about who gets to decide how art is presented, and about how long these works can remain in public spaces.

There was a time when the government dictated the direction of aesthetics. Only when the old order collapses do suppressed traditions find new life. Public buildings become canvases. Images naturally take on the role of narrative and expression. Murals spread across corridors and courtyards, functioning less like paintings meant to be admired and more like street signs or door plaques. Across different works, the same gestures appear again and again—heads raised, hands at labor, bodies in motion. Learning to read these images becomes part of life in the city and beyond. Through this art, Mexicans begin to build an entirely new sense of identity.

In technique, most of these works take the form of frescos. The painter works against the drying plaster. Pigments sink into the wall and allow almost no revision once set. Over time, colors gradually fade and outlines disappear beneath dust. Countless people pass beneath them, look up briefly, and walk on. Yet the walls remain, still bearing the traces.

Perhaps the mural's true significance lies not in its form or technique, but in the emotion and memory it carries.

The Story of the Sun Stone

The Aztec Sun Stone is often called the "Aztec Calendar." But it's really more of a cosmic map carved in basalt—or, as the Aztecs understood it, a guide to how the world works.

The stone was unearthed in Mexico City in the 18th century. It measures over 3.5 meters across and weighs more than 20 tons. The center of the Sun Stone is Tōnatiuh, the god of the sun. His gaze is stern, his outstretched tongue carved to resemble a Tecpatl. The message is clear: offer the sun your most precious gift—your blood—or receive nothing in return.

The concentric rings around Tōnatiuh record the four "suns" that came before—one transformed into a jaguar and devoured the people, one engulfed the world in a hurricane, one rained fire from the heavens, and the last drowned the world in a massive flood. Each sun's reign ended in an apocalypse, and none of their subjects survived.

Moving outward, you'll find religious symbols, patterns marking the cycle of day and night, and colors representing celestial bodies ... They unfold layer by layer, like a cosmic machine disassembled and laid bare—precise, ancient, orderly. Together, they capture the Aztec understanding of the world: the universe resets, all things are reborn, and humanity is nothing more than a speck of dust within it.

Murals and Turning Points

This is a land where traditions are told through murals. After the revolution, the young government turned to its artists. This newborn Mexico had so many stories to tell, so many to shape—and paintings adorning the walls of its buildings became the perfect medium. In the 1920s, the muralist movement swept through the country.

Look, this was an art form both ancient and brand new. It no longer lived in auction houses, galleries, or the private collections of the wealthy. Instead, it unfolded across vast walls open to the public. On those walls, artists spoke of justice, of freedom, of this nation's history and memory. Imagine it! A new country, a new canvas, and so many stories to tell! From the very beginning, these murals were inseparable from politics. The brush was the artist's voice. They spoke for their ideals, for beauty, for all the suffering people of the world ...

But voices are difficult to harmonize. And they can turn harsh.

As the 20th century entered its third decade, cracks began to appear—between artist and artist, between artist and state. Should the murals depict suffering or glory? Whose praises should they sing? Which path forward? Rivera, Orozco, and Siqueiros—three names that once symbolized hope, our "Los Tres Grandes"—held different visions for the future of both their art and their country.

The rifts only deepened. In the small "Midnight Kitchen," young painters listened to this "fight of the century."

Thousands of slot machines spitting out gold tokens, the glare of casino lights, the desert sun, and the old man's face shattering in sunlight. These images blend with the coin, with the halo over the "Mother's" head.
"I hope this is the last round."
*bang* The firing pin strikes. A bullet flies.
Primal instinct kicks in. Without even a fraction of a second to spare, Centurion tilts her head, just enough for the red-hot bullet to graze her scalp and slice through a few hairs.
The lead shot continues onward, striking obliquely against the wall of the alley before it ricochets beneath the hands of the saint herself.
The first gasps of surprise have barely had time to register what happened before the bullet rips through the man's body.
Interrogation Room, Police Station
It's all over.
The game ends. It's hard to say whose luck prevailed, but it's easy to tell who won. Mila is safe. The police have taken the man away, and Centurion takes back her lucky coin.
The police don't take long to finish their questioning. There is no lack of witnesses. But as Centurion heads for the door, she's handed a letter that Amador had left at the station.
An invitation to visit before she leaves town.
The outskirts fade into desert badlands, interrupted only by that narrow, babbling creek. No steam rises over the mint in the distance.
Centurion takes her time, letting her hands rest in her pockets, relaxed, until she reaches the cabin door.
"Mila, Amador—Huh?"
This time, the door with its worn white paint is not closed shut. It's swaying slightly with the breeze.
She peeks inside cautiously. Seeing no one, she clears her throat.
"Oh! Just a moment!"
Small, quick footsteps reveal the girl's approach.
"You actually came! I knew you would."
Mila's Home
"Ah, so that's why you didn't answer right away."
The living room is in complete disorder. Clothes, books, suitcases, and beat-up furniture fill the space. It looks nothing like her first visit.
Before Mila and Centurion arrived, Amador had been rushing to pack things.
"Sorry about the mess. Let me clear some of this."
Amador realizes he's making for a poor host. He moves a pile of clothes off the sofa so Centurion can sit.
Mila pulls her down and makes a pot of mint tea.
It's the same tea, with the same sweet flavor. But now the steam doesn't linger in the room. It rises and fades away, as if set free into the air.
Centurion sips her tea, then looks around and asks a question.
"Are you ...?"
"Uh, huh. It's exactly what it looks like."
"We're packing. We've decided to move."
Mila nods in agreement.
"After everything, it's probably for the best."
Centurion raises an eyebrow.
"Do you know where you're headed?"
"Not really. We just want to find our own path and see more of the world."
"I want to live somewhere with less struggle, where people won't look down on us."
"And where there are more possibilities, a place with more job opportunities and less fear."
The boy's face is determined, his gaze steady. But Mila looks down.
"It might not sound like much to you, but ..."
Mila looks up, her expression serious.
"This time, I want to try. I want to believe we can make it, because I've seen you do it."
"Still, it's scary. There are good people out there, but also bad ones. What if we're not strong enough?"
Mila seems to recall something. Her face brightens.
"But we're going to go see 'Mother' one last time before we leave!"
"She's listened before. It felt like a miracle. Maybe she'll watch over us on this journey too. I really want her blessing."
Centurion listens and then gives a confident, warm smile.
"Sounds like the start of something new. An adventure."
"Don't worry too much. You two will be fine. I wouldn't expect anything less of my dearest fans."
"If you want, you can take some luck from this old coin. Want to try?"
She takes out the familiar gold coin.
Mila takes it gingerly and holds the coin to her chest. She closes her eyes, squeezing her palm tight as if to wring some luck from it, then hands it back.
"I believe its luck will stick with me, just like it does with you."
Centurion nods and finishes her tea.
She opens her arms and hugs Mila, then nods to Amador.
"I'll let you get back to packing. It's been a while. I hope Jax hasn't forgotten about me."
"Señorita Centurion, can I ask you something?"
Mila looks down, twisting her hands shyly. Then she gathers her courage and asks a question.
"Why do you never seem to age?"
"Uncle Mario said you looked the same when he was a boy. Now, he's grown up, but you ... You're still the same."
Centurion crouches and pats Mila's shoulder.
"I once met an old man. We traded—my gold coin for his greatest treasure."
The ever-confident star winks.
"His gift was eternal youth, forever stuck at 19. Not a bad deal, since the coin only listens to me anyway."
It's the whole truth. But after hearing it, Mila slumps like a deflated balloon.
"I'm not a little kid anymore. You can't just make up stories like that."
Centurion laughs, then stands up to ruffle Mila's hair before turning to leave.
Centurion steps out of their house and walks alone far beyond the city's edge.
She passes beyond the Westside, through the ring of cacti, into the Sonoran Desert, just as she did before.
From day to night, something inside her pulls her here.
She stops and looks out at the dark horizon and the stars above.
What is luck? A coin? That halo around the mural? Or something unseen and intangible?
Will she ever find out?
No one can answer her.
Maybe no one needs to.
Centurion holds the coin she has carried since birth. She feels something vast inside her, as wide as the desert around her.
She stands still in the middle of the sand, feeling the enormous world turn beneath her feet.
If life is a gamble, she has always bet everything she has, never once hesitating.
Somehow, she knows that flip of the coin will always be on her side.
What else do you need? She tosses the gold coin toward the sky.
If you've got luck, you don't need a goddamn thing.

Marguerite has a habit of sneaking details about arcanists she has "studied" into her own profile, waiting for someone to notice. Unfortunately, as of today, no one has. The only attention she gets is from the leader of the "Storm" research team, of all people, who hands her a 50 Sharpodonty coupon for the canteen—a gesture of "humanitarian concern."|Eagle presents her with a French horn she has been secretly preparing for a long time. Marguerite accepts the gift with a smile. She later tells Eagle, though, that their objective of sneaking into the concert isn't to perform.|On the way to Institutum Lorentz, Marguerite "receives" a strawberry steak that drops from the sky, an explosive balloon filled with combustible gas, and an Auto-Winder Critter that can sing "Happy Birthday." She feels this is more like a torture session designed by X rather than a birthday celebration.
A chaos researcher who walks alone through the rain. An assassin who unravels the threads of fate. One of your most elusive friends.

There was a time when she used chilaquiles as a birthday cake—hands and feet bumping into each other in a cramped space, simple wishes and laughter ringing in her ears. She thought she had long forgotten all of it, until she realized it was this very memory that healed the wounds on her hands and in her heart. Only then did she realize it had been there all along, hidden in the back of her mind.|From Recoleta, Ramona learned more metaphors for life. Life begins with a cry and ends with a sigh. The days in between are like children darting down a street—gone in a flash. And so she began to wear commemorative flowers to mark the date, adorning herself, her days, and her life.|A letter reached her through the Vigiles Bureau. One glance at the postmark and the handwriting, and she knew exactly who had sent it. Before she could open it, her friends in the Suitcase spotted the birthday wishes on the back of the envelope and broke into celebration. As the letter itself put it, it was already a gift. Whether she ever actually read it, though, remains a mystery.
An exorcist who strays far from the crowd, walking the night with ghosts as her companions. One of your most talented friends when it comes to the art of saying "goodbye."
Lady by the Lake

She can't remember the last time she celebrated her birthday. Today, the moment she opens her three eyes, gentle morning light greets her. It's dawn inside the Suitcase, but this time she isn't alone in the dark anymore. This small happiness is enough to bring her to tears.|Lady by the Lake remembers one particular day. In a silent, dust-covered warehouse, an arcane clockwork suddenly burst into song, throwing everything into a stir. She was disappointed to learn afterward that it had only been an accident, not an encounter with a fellow Awakened. But that brief moment of chaos still glows warmly in her memory.|A warm and friendly art salon is held inside the Suitcase. Lady by the Lake sits on a green meadow in the Wilderness, spending the day discussing the many interpretations of lines and planes with her friends, imagining the trends of the future. Her form isn't for everyone, and not every kind of art that others appreciate makes sense to her. But to gather together and share a view as beautiful as the one she saw when she first awakened—that alone is precious enough.

Additive Manufacturing Device

A Demonic Scale-based additive manufacturing machine, powered by tens of thousands of arcane skills operating simultaneously.
Every arcane skill within the printer is interconnected. Even the slightest deviation in initial conditions can lead to drastically different results.
According to the interviewee, the device can provide whatever help is needed—whether it's a sniper rifle or a toaster.
Liquid Metal-Coated "Glove"

A pair of gloves with a metallic sheen, shimmering like the scales on a butterfly's wings.
Though the interviewee described them as the arms of an Awakened, we know they are simply the latest product of the LSCC—refined, of course, by Institutum Lorentz.
"ID"

She can be Ms. Jones, Special Investigator of the St. Pavlov Foundation, or Marguerite, researcher of the Laplace Scientific Computing Center. Any identity will do, as long as it opens the right doors.
The Beginning of Chaos

Eras bounce like marbles—backward, forward, backward again. Mostly backward, right?
She learned what 1999's Cambridge had to teach her. Her gift allows her to pick up on patterns intuitively, but her nature ensures she will always be a skeptic. And here lies the paradox that the rise and fall of eras brings—one that traps everyone who still remembers, who still thinks: Are we moving forward or backward? What can we hold on to?
Yes, the storms of an era are always more interesting than still water. Rather than clinging to a single foothold, she would rather leap with the times, joining in the dangerous game of takeoffs and landings.
So where is the butterfly that first fluttered its wings?
If you want to hide a leaf, the best place is a forest. If you want to hide a brilliant mind, the best place is Laplace. Yes, it is the temple of science—but the science it commands cannot answer the great questions of its era. That alone can trigger a collapse of faith. Fortunately, she was never attached to any of it.
When neat theories crumble with the era, a butterfly stirs its wings among the rubble, flying into endless chaos.

Afflatus: Guiding Herb [Plant] Exorcist
Agave Incense

Incense woven from agave leaves, sage, mugwort, and other plants, handmade by the interviewee.
Its existence defies two traditions: for those who handle ghosts, agave leaves hold no exorcism powers; for ordinary people, the value of agave lies in its fruit.
And so the leaves were left by the roadside. The passing exorcist picked them up, saving them from being swallowed up by the dust.
AM Radio

A gift from a foreign land, given by her parents out of well-meaning concern.
To coax open a path into her heart, they offered her a piece of the world's noise. She discovered on her own that the sun disrupts radio waves. To get a clear signal, she usually goes out at night, seeking open high ground to tune in to her favorite music.
When the ionosphere interferes with the signal, the music twists and warps—occasionally shrieking like a ghost. But in that distortion, she finds peace. Real peace.
Miguel Candle

A candle etched with ancient incantations, preserving the hours spent turned inward.
The interviewee shows little enthusiasm for her craft—to her, exorcism is just a job to be done. When asked whether she invests much care in her exorcism tools, she again replied "No." But when hard work doesn't feel like misery, perhaps that's a kind of love.
Faded Childhood

The family—mother, father, and daughter—all crammed inside a tiny twenty-square meter house.
Fate did not bless them with much, but they made up for it with optimism. They got by, and their days were filled with laughter.
In their free time—and time was the one thing they had plenty of—the afternoon sun would slip through the narrow window around five or six o'clock, dust drifting in the light. They would watch their daughter run from one corner of the room to the other. They didn't understand her strange behavior then and simply chalked it up to a child's game.
Outside, the world was racing forward into the future. New systems, new schools, new breakfasts, trains bound for foreign lands—everything appeared as if from a dream. They refused to stand on the sidelines, having their lives dictated by interest payments.
One day, they opened the door to find their unusually quiet daughter huddled in a corner. She told them there were ghosts in the house. In that instant, her strange behavior made sense.
What a great discovery!
Like voyagers finding a new continent, they pried open the shell of their ordinary lives and looked up to see a new sky. With a little creative reframing, their story became one of a long-forgotten bloodline regaining its power. In an age when priests had retreated behind the curtain, and sacred hymns survived only in archives, a new "psychic family" was destined to rise.
A reputable newspaper published their lies. Under the journalist's gifted pen, their daughter became a small-time "exorcist." They moved into a new home, full of light, and time grew scarce.
But why was their daughter becoming more withdrawn? Why did she keep hiding in corners and cabinets?
No matter. In horror films, the odd one out is often the greatest survivor!
Fragments of Life

... May 31, 1915. She had three hours to complete Mr. Andrew's commission at a cornfield fifteen miles away. Their car rattled along the edge of the desert before finally reaching their destination. Mr. Andrew explained that an evil spirit was haunting the cornfield and disrupting road construction. He needed her to finish the exorcism in two hours. "Efficiency! That's what matters!" She spotted a villager hiding behind a pile of construction materials. She was clever enough to know the truth—that was the real "ghost." June 4, 1915. An urgent commission: an evil spirit had appeared in Captain Miguel's house. His family suspected it was his dead colleague. Her parents claimed this job was a rush order, so they charged double. By then, she could sense spirits using exorcism herbs and her arcane skill. The ghost hiding in the wardrobe wasn't trying to hurt the captain. It was weeping from fear and loneliness. She performed the standard exorcism. The captain offered no word of thanks. February 3, 1916. New magazines and newspapers arrived in town. A publication called Portrait requested an interview with her. At her parents' urging, the feature was slated for the cover. She ran outside and hid in the shadows where no one would notice her. She whispered to the world, "Quiet. Please be quiet." After that, she decided to tell everyone she couldn't hear the ghosts' voices. ...
Be Quiet, Would You Kindly?

Pandora Wilson: Hmm? Ms. Ramona, are you preparing a ritual?
Pandora Wilson: Didn't the Vigiles Bureau explain that this mouth is an arcane skill, not a ghost?
Ramona: Of course, I can see and hear you.
Ramona: I guess the Vigiles Bureau didn't tell you I enjoy a little practical joke every now and then.
Pandora Wilson: I was briefed on that, but seeing it in person is different. Your humor is all about the delivery and timing, it seems.
Pandora Wilson: Like just now. Dropping a joke right at the start of an interview certainly catches a person off guard.
Ramona: I never thought "humor" could be analyzed.
Pandora Wilson: Of course it can. It's just a social tool. People use it to soothe their nerves and ease the tension. It seems you don't enjoy interviews.
Ramona: I wouldn't say I like them much.
Pandora Wilson: Then is it safe to say you are quite comfortable with yourself and don't see anxiety as a weakness you need to hide?
Ramona: Hmm ... You've got a real talent for analysis. Still, calling it out like that is a little ...
Pandora Wilson: Embarrassing?
Ramona: Humorless.

The Boundary of a Painting

A simple wooden frame, assembled sometime after 1914.
Over the course of its turbulent life, it was accidentally stained with a distinctive blue oil paint—stubborn, viscous, and difficult to clean, though not impossible to remove.
Does a painting need its frame, or does a frame need its painting? She spent her long years in storage turning this question over, and she can't wait to hear what our readers think.
"Differences in Perspective"

The interviewee's eyes share a single plane yet look in different directions. All welcome a visitor's gaze. When eyes meet, thoughts spark—and the canvas finds its meaning in the viewer's presence.
The interviewee believes she can be read in many ways. A multi-angled perspective is what she loves most, though she'd never insist it's the only way in.
"Spring, 1912"

One of the things stored within the interviewee—and one of the few she treasures.
The photo captures a single moment: young painters yearning to interpret the world through a new vision. Then came war, poverty, new techniques ... Life pulled them apart, and their names have long since been lost. But these faces are still treasured within her.
Multifaceted Expression

She blinks her three eyes.
In the first two decades of the twentieth century, the cafés of Paris were never without flowers. Young artists debated the nature of painting and of things themselves: the world was changing so fast. The traditional craft of reproducing objects on canvas had been perfected—yet it no longer felt new. In the face of the camera's challenge, what was the point of a paintbrush?
The young painters answered with lines, planes, and geometric forms—broken apart and rebuilt.
She has seven profiles, a beautiful hat, and a pool of spring water. They exist across different times and angles. The young man who came to Paris wielding his charcoal sticks, hungry to make the human eye seize the beauty around him all at once. She was meant to be multi-perspectival, anti-traditional, real, and yet beyond real—a vision made by artist and viewer together.
She remembers that café. Quiet and elegant, the air thick with the scent of coffee and books. Snatches of conversation drifted past, and she was glad when someone paused to look—at the lake, the clouds, the very essence of clouds, all rendered on a single plane.
Oh, my dear friend—how wonderful that you share this curiosity. Cubism, as the name suggests ...
How she wanted to be part of the conversation. The world is vast and subtle and endlessly fascinating. There is so much an artist can do, so much worth saying! This is Paris—everyone here has an artistic vision to voice, everyone a world of their own to imagine.
People stopped. They looked. They bought her. And her voice was swallowed up.
The Belle Époque was slipping away.
An awakened painting. A painting that could hold so much, and hide more. Beyond Cubism, she has become something far more interesting.
The Art of Tomorrow

June X, 1912
I don't like Paris. Too many people. Too many voices. Too many ... things. Everyone has their own opinion on how to paint. Mr. Antoine caught me at the apartment door and held me there through the whole lecture. He told me he didn't like those little cubes—as if I didn't agree, he'd have my two months' rent on the spot.
In Paris, answers are never in short supply. But what exactly is the question?

September X, 1912
Good news: I have a job! For at least three months, I will be teaching students the fundamentals of art at the studio. I won't have to worry about where my next meal is coming from.
Samuel says I spent twelve hours yesterday staring at a pipe. He's exaggerating.

October X, 1913
I'm a fool. I still don't know how to paint. Deconstruct a bowl of fruit, a violin, or a model into eighty planes and flatten them onto a single canvas—is that the question, or the answer?

April X, 1914
I've left Paris ... I have to get as far away as I can before I change my mind. I didn't say goodbye to anyone. And yet it's still a cliché: a change of scenery—going off into nature to find inspiration. Yes, always nature. I don't have a mind as clever as Mr. Picasso's or Mr. Braque's. All I can do is throw myself into the cliché.
I'm heading to the lakes. May the green of Lake Annecy give me that answer—or at least tell me what game my fickle Muse is playing.

May X, 1914
A lake. The answer is a lake. The question is a lake.
Nothing more.
A Conversation Enthusiast

Pandora Wilson: Just as I mentioned, our readers want to know the real you. Feel free to say whatever's on your mind—I mean, relax.
Lady by the Lake: Oui, of course, and merci. You needn't explain what an interview is to me. I'm just—oh, please forgive me; I'm simply too excited! You came here to have a conversation with me ... with me ... Good heavens!
Pandora Wilson: You seem excited at the opportunity for a conversation.
Lady by the Lake: It's true. You see, I rarely get the chance, Ms. Wilson. Before entering the Timekeeper's Suitcase, the place I knew best was a dusty warehouse. Those few people that visited there seldom felt the need to talk to a painting.
Pandora Wilson: You've listened and experienced so much. I'm sure our readers are curious.
Lady by the Lake: How kind of you to say so. Let me think ... Perhaps "witnessed" or "carried" would be more accurate than "experienced." I keep things hidden for people—things both precious and discarded; so many little unremarkable things. I always make note of their stories. Something to pass the time on those long and quiet days.
Pandora Wilson: And how about your story?
Lady by the Lake: It's hardly worth telling. But ...
Lady by the Lake: Every painting longs to be seen. To have someone to talk to. I've always wondered what different viewers find in me—the complete picture of "me" can only take shape inside the viewer's mind. And if a viewer were willing to share what they see ... that would be wonderful indeed!
Lady by the Lake: I even have a list of topics! We could talk about art, or the different ways profiles can be combined, or spring ...
"Fresh Vision" Omni-Easel

Crafted from stained glass with exceptional light transmission and brass commonly used in ley line surveying instruments.
It is said to be a popular sketching aid among scholars of ley lines. It grants the artist a unique perspective—one that reaches "deeper than reality."
The Pigments' Sanctum

A well-worn sketchbook—the perfect sanctum for arcane pigments.
Having fed on her thoughts and inspiration, the images these pigments produce are startlingly vivid. They leap off the page and beckon.
The Other Canvas

It allows the interviewee to cast aside her usual caution, leaving spontaneous splashes of color along her hem.
After all, this is how stars and clouds are scattered across the canvas of the cosmos—just as nostalgia and longing settle into her blue eyes.
Proof of Countless Conceptions

Exclusive to the curator, this identification grants access to the exhibition hall before and after shows.
Through countless moments of contemplation, she draws every point between artist and viewer into a single line—ensuring that every brushstroke and color reaches the audience's retinas without obstruction. Through her hands, the artist's inner world is stitched into an exhibition that can be experienced.
The Burning "Veins"

A silk scarf with a pearlescent sheen, accompanied by a card from a viewer.
Red seeps along the veins of the petals, like the blood vessels of a bouquet. Yet from a distance, they seem to simply burn in silence.
Personal Shawl

A shawl hand-stitched by the interviewee herself. Warm, neat, and easy to move in.
Against her formal attire, the shawl betrays a glimpse of her personality. She favors intricate stitching and seems to work through tangled, bitter problems as her needle moves. The time it takes to finish a shawl is enough to unravel several difficult thoughts.
Ultramarine Droplets

A blue tear, frozen at the corner of the interviewee's eye.
In the silence of her downcast gaze, the writer lets go of the urge to ask what pigment gives this blue its shade. Even if ultramarine is no longer precious, a mother's tears are worth their weight in gold.
Thorned Halo

A headscarf that should be soft and white, adorned instead with sharp, black thorns—their lines like the marks left by a lash.
Its maker believes a mother should teach her children the shape of thorns early, even if it might prick their fingers.
In Her Embrace

A bundle, gently soothed without end. The key resting on it trembles with each touch. "It really is a good child—insisting on keeping my key safe in its own way."
A mother always accepts her child's kindness, and the interviewee is no exception.
"The Ever-Blooming"

A flower that will never wither, pieced together from wire, scraps of cloth, and thread.
So cheap, so clumsy, so insignificant—and yet so precious, sincere and enduring.
Sewing Kit

A carefully maintained toolkit, though years of use have left their mark.
"We use it to mend clothes and stitch stage backdrops. Sometimes, we weave a dream with it."
A Blurry Portrait

A portrait of a woman in white. Her face and clothing are indistinct.
Is she imaginary or real? Is the interviewee turning away from this face, or longing for the woman in the portrait to step forward and be reunited?
In the interviewee's silence, there is no answer.

Hippie's Notes

What a terrible place!
I don't want to think about any of it—how I thought I'd gotten away from that island, only to wind up back in the Manus's hands ... I spent every penny on custom-made clothes to show respect for the island's philosopher, yet didn't come across a single Dionysan believer in the end! Is art truly dying? The people here only care about cannons and warships. Not one of them would stop to listen.
But it gets worse: even when I found kindred spirits, I couldn't stay in touch with them—all because of the Manus. Their words are so tempting that even I nearly lost myself in those seemingly beautiful descriptions.
Fortunately, a sweet-smelling lady came to my aid. She told me some truths and helped me persuade a few fine people to support my work, allowing my art to take root here—fine, even if those people understand nothing about art!
The path of great art is always winding—but the future is bright.

There is a strange girl in the Youth Palace of Sparrow Hills.
She always wears traditional dress, eyes closed, as though she has never quite woken up. She appears in the most unexpected places—the peak of Sparrow Hills, the clothesline, even the highest rooftop of the Youth Palace. After a while, no one thinks much of it. She is an arcanist, after all, and arcanists always have their reasons.
The children grow used to her, pinning fresh flowers to her collar. Over time, they start to call her their "Sleepy Friend" and invite her to join their evening tea parties of shadow-puppet rabbits, colorful desserts, and top-hatted guests. And of course, that drowsy "Alice" is always there among them.

"Enough work for today. Leave the next eight hours to me." The door to the workers' club swings open, and a wave of warm air wraps around Oliver Fog, sealing him off from the bitter cold of the Siberian winter. As always, the room smells like old books and cinders. Not far from the entrance, a few men lean over a chessboard. "Sicilian Defense," perhaps—he wouldn't know; Oliver has never been much of a chess player. The two players sit with furrowed brows, mulling over each move longer and longer as the game unfolds. Oliver pulls a sweet from his pocket and pops it into his mouth. Off to the side, someone fumbles with an accordion, playing a haphazard rendition of Moscow Nights. The song is everywhere these days. Imagine it—if one day no one has to work at all, and we could just enjoy moments like this ... how wonderful that would be. He places a hand on the cat curled at his side and strokes it, gently, trying not to disturb the moment.

The research vessel is about to set sail for the North Pole!
By nightfall, almost everyone is talking about the news. What will the scientists uncover this time in that distant, frozen land? Its ecosystems, its indigenous peoples and their cultures, or the truths of ancient myths?
Even the arcanist celebrity Eternity cannot resist spending a small fortune and joining the voyage.
For a woman who has seen as much as she has, the journey is more of a rare indulgence than an investment. The world has long failed to surprise her, but the North still holds its secrets.
For better or worse, she is on the move again—drawn not only by profit, but by the thrill of stepping into the unknown.

There is no peace and quiet when Medicine Pocket is around.
They care little for social etiquette, constantly tearing apart whatever room they are in and making sure everyone is aware of their displeasure. At the appraisal, everyone votes to name them "Employee of the Year" so they can be given a soundproof office of their own.
Rare as it is, Medicine Pocket is finally satisfied with their surroundings, so much so that they actually sit down and work in silence for hours.
Absorbed in their experiments, they hardly notice a passing painter, who pauses to capture the scene and later names it "A Peaceful Researcher."
Introduce a little obstacle into their chain of logic.
Rain, Chaos, and Fluttering
The world itself is a synthesis of chaos.
She never lets her work grow stale.
Between Spirits and Blossoms
The unheard and the unseen all find their way to her.
She just wants a room where she won't feel alone.
Birth of Spring
When the lake is only a lake. When she is only herself.
Her ideal world lies on the other side of the stained glass.

It's a fine afternoon. Sunlight spills across the palette, catching Tyrian purple with a faint glow. Centuries ago, this color could only be extracted from murex snails. The color's rarity made it the emblem of royalty and nobility. Now, it sits on a shelf in an ordinary shop.
When she first started learning to paint, she was always too caught up in proportion and accuracy. Afraid of making mistakes, she hesitated before every stroke. Then one day, a hand reached from behind, grasped her brush, and drew the first line across the canvas.
"Ms. Vila?" She turned to find her art teacher.
"There's no rush, Comrade Kiperina," came a gentle but firm voice. "Be bold. Precise measurement isn't always the answer in art and aesthetics."
"Then again ..." her teacher's eyes flickered. "Your measuring method is very unique. I've seen another comrade use it before, and I believe it can be quite a useful aid."
Crying, wailing, tears about to fall, arms reaching for hope ... Words have no power here.

What can save a ruined painting?
Fragments of a renowned work drift through the air—a bull with its head raised, a neighing horse, a mother cradling her dead child, a soldier's corpse still clutching a broken sword. A bulb flickers among them like an all-seeing eye. The painting captures a military bombardment. Beneath the shriek of artillery, the people of northern Spain were brought low.
People say she is preparing an exhibition about death—an omen in itself. When she pulls the final string taut, the fragments will rise and lock together in the air, forming a panorama of this senseless tragedy ... A tragedy she will depict in full during the coming exhibition.
She will hang it in the most prominent corner of the gallery.
Because sacrifice must never be forgotten.
Cold Cradle
She hums a somber lullaby—a mother's way to soothe her trembling, heart-pierced child.

Death, resurrection, new life.
Ascetics in pointed hats, attendants bearing candles, the Madonna robed in splendor ... The procession moves slowly, in silence and solemnity, spreading through the street.

There is no end to the festivities beneath the marigolds of Tenochtitlán.
Your Suitcase is an interesting place, Timekeeper. The chaotic energy here feels stronger than anywhere else I've been.
My Rumbling Roaring Box is always going off.
Unfortunately, I still haven't reached the lake where the Spinning Wheel is.
Every time I get close, I black out.
Maybe you know how I can get to the Wheel?
Yes, but the problem is there are too many "treasures" here.
They've kept me from finding the real secret.
Since you're the owner of all these "treasures," can you give me a hint?
Timekeeper, do you want me to perform an exorcism on the Wilderness?
It's never quiet here, day or night.
... Just kidding.
I wasn't actually gonna ward off our friends in the Suitcase.
So, were they actually willing to watch a horror movie with me again?
After the movie last night, I told the group that someone had been sitting in the corner, watching with us the whole time ...
They didn't look happy about it.
Timekeeper! I'm here!
Being able to see you every day is my greatest fortune! Please stay and chat with me again.
Of course!
The breeze, the rain, the sunrises, the sunsets ... I could stay in the Wilderness all day!
And best of all, there are so many friends around all the time!
The girl who writes stories, the researcher with little snakes on her head, the young lady who makes potions ...
They can talk with me all day long.
There's nothing better than good conversation!
Timekeeper, I noticed you've never told the others in the Suitcase my true identity.
Why are you keeping my secret?
True. But I didn't expect you to be so straightforward about it.
These surprises are exactly what I was hoping for.
I'm glad we are in agreement.
Then maybe you'd like to come to some ... private meetings of Institutum Lorentz?
You always rush by. You almost never stay.
Being the Timekeeper seems harder than I thought.
... Vertin, you must be joking, right?
Taking care of every one of your friends visiting the Suitcase, setting up the hall, preparing the Insight rituals ... only you can do these things.
Then let's gather some Fox Tails together!
Once the herb is ready, I can sew its flowers into gloves and shoes for you.
That will hide your trail. Then no one will know you're taking a little break ...
Vertin, come here!
I have some small gifts for you to celebrate our time together as friends.
This is a grain of salt I found near the Wishing Spring ... Maybe it's from a Salted Mandrake?
And a little hat made from Critter fluff!
How curious. It smells like Dust.
Yes, you're right ... We still have a long, long time ahead of us.
And many, many more stories to share!
Did you find something?
It's like a treasure hunt.
They're not evil spirits. They're our friends.
I was asked to invite you to a horror-themed party tonight.
Are you accustomed to the Suitcase now?
Have you made new friends recently?
Maybe you saw this coming.
I find it more fun this way.
You can help me with it.
I can stay with you a little.
What gifts?
You don't have to be so polite.

How does one join the Laplace Scientific Computing Center?
It depends. If you ask the Staff Committee, you'll receive the official response: we accept applications from both humans and arcanists, as long as your research does not focus solely on technology or arcanum alone.
Of course, as an institution operating under the jurisdiction of the Pax Security Council, Laplace has always concentrated its research efforts on the fusion of technology and arcanum. But when it comes to hiring its staff, does the computing center have any de facto, unwritten requirements in place? We asked some of its researchers to find out.

Anonymous Researcher A: Join us? Are you crazy? Are you a genius? No? Then forget it.
Anonymous Researcher B: That's not the only way. You could also—
Anonymous Researcher A: Oh! Do you have a fishbowl for a head? Do you need to plug yourself in to stay charged? Are you a crow?
Anonymous Researcher B: ... Stop that, you're ruining Laplace's reputation in front of the press! And Ludwig is a raven. A raven! Not a crow!
"Language Disorder"

What if one day everyone around you started communicating only in symbols? Menus in binary code. News written in sudoku. Waiters speaking in a mix of Arabic and Roman numerals. What would you do?
I would go to my room, close my eyes, and hope I'd wake up from this nightmare soon.
At Laplace, this "Language Disorder" really happened, but the "mad" geniuses of the LSCC figured out how to communicate anyway. When everyday words and speech turned into ciphers, the researchers cracked the codes and went back to their normal routines ...
And that's why I'm sitting here writing articles while they're on the cutting edge of arcane and human progress.
Of course, that disaster has since been resolved. I heard they even took the opportunity to make new discoveries and submit papers on the topic. While the scientific details are still top secret, I have faith these "mad" researchers have come up with something genius.
For Those Who Have Departed

The Foundation held a solemn memorial for Madam Greta Hofmann. The ceremony praised her contribution to the discovery of the "Hofmann Knot" in a great many words. Yet, as I put these thoughts to paper, I find myself returning to Ms. Marcus's expression most of all. As she delivered her eulogy at the burial, I saw tenderness and sorrow, but also the determination to move forward.
Move forward. A simple, two-word concept. And yet, it's also a complex one. Move forward to where? Which way is forward? What lies ahead? Those of us in the "present" will never know for sure.
Madam Greta Hofmann's younger brother, Mr. Adler Hofmann, currently works at Laplace, but he did not attend the ceremony or the burial. While it has been some time since Madam Lucy resigned as director of Laplace, her seat remains empty. It seems that Laplace has yet to propose a suitable candidate. How will the LSCC move forward from here?
To that end, we can't help but wonder: what about Mr. Enigma, the third contributor to the "Hofmann Knot"?
A Shadow Inside the Box

Note: This is a special submission that was delivered anonymously on behalf of the author. While the sender's address is located in Laplace, the author is not a Laplace employee. Refusing to reveal the author's identity, the sender claimed the author had no name, or her name had been forgotten. Perhaps she isn't even real—just a fragment of a dream, or the moon drifting over a sleepless night. Once, I could not trust my own memory. Everything around me kept shifting, reverting ... resetting. Perhaps this was a lesson that belonged only to the waking or the "gods." It should not have touched me. I should not have written this. I should have continued appearing at the right time, in the right place, reciting lines others had written for me. But my memories remained. I began to wonder. I began to think. Is this a gift? Whether it was an accident or a coincidence, I believe this ability to "think" was only bestowed upon me. When words are isolated and thoughts are stolen, false omniscience regresses everyone into tools. Yet they call this the only way to survive the "Storm." I have only just begun to truly think, but that mad raven seeks to rob everyone of their thoughts. He claims it is the ultimate solution. Death, or a tortured, twisted life? I would choose the former without hesitation.
From Musae III

A philosopher from your homeland once said, "If we take a foot-long stick and cut it in half each day, we will never reach its end."
No, I'm not here to discuss calculus. I'd like to ask you this: Do you think a stick can truly be divided forever? If you reach the point where it can no longer be halved, what remains?
You might say it's some fundamental particle, but in my class, the correct answer is a string.
Nature's most basic unit is not a particle but an incredibly tiny string. Divide a stick to its limit, and you'll find a string. Divide gold down to its limit, and you'll also find a string. Even the basic unit of gravity should be a string.
The entire world is made of strings vibrating at different frequencies in unseen, higher dimensions. They may seem insignificant, but they are everywhere.

Beginner's Guide to Ciphers: Vigenère Edition

To prevent Laplace employees from falling victim to pranks from colleagues and to avoid research delays from being unable to break codes, we are distributing this Beginner's Guide to Ciphers: Vigenère Edition.
The Vigenère cipher can be seen as an upgrade to the Caesar cipher, turning the simple shift of a single alphabet into shifts across multiple alphabets to increase complexity. For more on the Caesar cipher, see the Caesar Cipher Edition.
The main difference between the Vigenère and Caesar ciphers is that in the Vigenère cipher, the relationship between the ciphertext and plaintext letters isn't one-to-one, making the key harder to figure out. However, since it still follows patterns, you can still find repeating ciphertext segments. By using high-frequency words in common language, you can guess the plaintext for specific segments of ciphertext, deduce the key length from the spacing between repeats, and analyze the key.
However, if you don't have much text, this can be difficult. In these situations, you should use other methods to guess the key. The personality, past, and writing habits of the person who made the code are important clues. Here is a list of people at Laplace who are very likely to play pranks with ciphers: Adler, Ulrich, X, Richard, Dawkins, Victor ... If you encounter a prank, consider these suspects first. If you can't crack the code, confront the suspects directly and ask them to stop the prank. If a suspect denies involvement, try to force them to decode it for you. It doesn't matter whether they're really the culprit or not.

After the ninth "Storm," Musae III provided the toybox as a tool for simulation experiments to help develop a Pre-Storm Emergency Protocol that meets LSCC standards while adhering to humanitarian principles.
Note: Existing solutions all failed to meet LSCC standards. Based on the scientific principles of "objective investigation, rational skepticism, pluralistic doubt, and equal debate," response plans for the "Storm" should also be tested in practice. The Year Order Failed

Like many who live through a turning point in history, people did not notice right away that the world had shifted from its original course.

Before the "Storm" arrived, it seemed that everything could be calculated. Cause led to effect in predictable ways. The truth hid inside formulas and proofs, just waiting for those patient and brilliant enough to reveal it. The city shone with steady, controlled lights. Machines worked with a quiet rhythm. The future felt like a blank answer sheet lying on the table, ready to be filled in.

But the "Storm" defied all reason. It swept away not only roads and eras, but also the presuppositions people once believed could never change. Physics lost its regularity. Reason no longer guaranteed conclusions. Well-established systems collapsed in the face of reversing time. People started talking about "adapting," about "reorienting," as if a change of vocabulary could reframe this chaos into progress.

This era no longer values certainty. Order has taken a back seat. Answers are viewed as outdated luxuries. The world has begun championing variable, ambiguous, inexplicable things. Those still clinging to order are like leftover variables in an old equation—unable to be integrated, yet impossible to cancel out.

Time, however, keeps moving. It does not wait for understanding or pause for formulas that no longer work. Like an undulating tide, it pushes some people into the unknown, and it leaves others behind. Those who remain are left probing the same question over and over, hoping to prove its solvability.

Since that year, the world no longer promises the existence of a right answer.
It only asks that people keep trying to find one.

A girl stands in the sitting room under a gleaming crystal chandelier. Layers upon layers of lace form the skirt of her dress, each pleat perfectly ironed flat. She clenches her hands, rubbing her fingers along the seams.
At this moment, a girl named Sophie is waiting for the Rosenkavalier to arrive.
The door opens. A young man holding a silver rose hurries inside. His light footsteps strike against the polished floor, echoing throughout the silent room.
Sophie lifts her head. She sees his hand tremble as it holds onto the flower and his eyes glisten in the glittering light. The silver rose at his chest shines like a drop of moonlight plucked from the night sky.
"I ..."
They both begin to speak, then stop at the same time.
Sophie looks down and holds the rose closer. She allows a smile to slip onto her face, then she starts to sing the words of a song that everyone knows.
Sophie the maiden and the Rosenkavalier create a beautiful duet, forming a shining moment in the play.

The heavy church gates softly shut behind her. Expelled for violating the convent's moral strictures, Sister Osmina of Suor Angelica has found herself cast out of her sanctuary. With nowhere to go, she makes her way down the stone stairs with her head bowed. But then, she catches the fragrance of flowers in the air. As she lifts her head, she sees a lush garden before her. In stark contrast to the solemn church, the garden overflows with vibrant roses. Bathed in the afternoon sunlight, bees dart between the blooms, their wings laden with golden dust. Fallen petals blanket the grass in a thick, velvety carpet. As another breeze sweeps past, a few stray petals drift down to rest upon her shoulders. God may have barred them from His sanctuary, yet the roses care little, blooming with wild, reckless abandon. She stands and lingers there for some time, long enough for the setting sun to stretch her shadow across the earth. Clinging to the cold stone wall, she simply watches the flowers in silence. Not a single prayer crosses her lips.

Act IV The Castle Garden, Cloaked in Night In the serene moonlight, the maiden's veil shimmers like liquid silver. The heavy, sweet scent of rose garlands drift across the lush lawn. "The moment of bliss draws nigh, how sweet my lover's embrace—" Is the soprano's aria truly that enchanting, or has her arcane skill already captivated the crowd? Entranced by the romantic melody, not a single soul in the audience notices that Susanna has vanished from the stage. At that exact moment, thousands of miles away, a museum's most prized collection vanishes into the ether. Once again, a brilliantly bizarre heist has been flawlessly executed. It was a perfect crime, naturally. After all, who would've ever suspected that the prop necklace around the prima donna's throat had been seamlessly swapped for the genuine one?

As the lights dim, a forest materializes from the shadows.
Perched upon a bough, the bird catcher in green raises a pan flute to her lips, breathing the first note into being. The melody takes flight, drifting into the distance like a luminous sequence of prime numbers. Soon after, a faint, trilling answer echoes back from the depths of the foliage.
In the auditorium, the audience holds its breath, terrified that a single sigh might startle the distant unseen flock.
As if on cue, the birds appear: a dazzling, iridescent, radiant flurry. Woven from the very essence of twilight, they flutter right down to center stage. One clumsy little creature takes a tumble, falling perfectly into the bird catcher's waiting hand.
With the click of a camera shutter from a mezzanine box, this fleeting scene is captured for all eternity.
First, the world falls apart, followed by reason. And only then do questions begin to surface.

The flame of her candle persists against the dark. As she softly cups her hands around it, the light seems to emanate from her palms like a sacred flame conjured by Hestia herself. It is this gentleness, this tenacity, and this endless courage that form the core of her limitless strength.
And so tonight, holding her lamp, she humbly steps into the dark where the shadows lie in wait.

During a night at a campsite in Cuernavaca, accompanied by a poet's song, a young writer set off on a winding journey. She later arrived at a textile factory, where a rebellion from its female workers brought an end to that brief yet brutal job. On a ship headed to Buenos Aires, the wide Río de la Plata witnessed her great dream of becoming a sailor.
In the end, she did not become one. Instead, she wrote a short poem on the ship. It was an imperfect work, one with an inconsistent meter and nonexistent rhyming scheme. Yet in her journey of self-discovery, these moments of chaos were nothing more than splashes of water in the long, twisting river of self-actualization.
After all the struggles, the hardships, and the foolish, fearless adventures, the young writer has arrived here at last. She pushes open the door in front of her. In her mind, the door shines with glittering green gems and gleaming gold. In the real world, it is plain and ordinary. But from behind the door, you can just barely catch the sound of crashing waves and a glimpse of a far-off lighthouse. It is a good place to think and write.
Dear little writer, from now on, I hope you always have a room of your own.

The metal shines with a cold silver light, pointing proudly at the sky. Inside the tall building at the harbor, the redesigned ship in a bottle waits, excited, for the time of the launch.

The building roars. The ground shakes. Grayish white smoke fills the air. Bright red flames form a tail behind the ship.
There she goes! Her destination? The future!

Today's most important result: our last results were wrong.
Alright, time for the "Anything Goes" phase of the experiment.
Stop asking. There's a systematic error playing tricks on me.
We skipped this step. Surely nobody will notice ... right?
I have an idea—maybe this will work!
These results ... I can't even pretend to understand them.
We conducted this experiment three times, and the results were all identical ... Identically wrong.
Another day, another step closer to the answer.
It's hard to say whether I'm actually doing anything useful.
I've got so many good ideas!
If the control group performs too well, there's no point in testing the treatment group.
I'll put these parameters in the "Presentable" file.
If we keep at it, we might make a breakthrough at any moment!
Finding the source of a problem is also progress.
Yes! That's it! I knew I wasn't wrong!
The data looks good, but we could definitely make it sound more impressive.
I hereby dub this phenomenon "Schrödinger's Reproducibility."
Let's do a test run first. If it works, we'll have solved half the problem already.
I've already done so much work today. I could probably clock out right now!
It's just like I said: there's a problem here! Time to fix it!
Perhaps we can implement this time-delay mechanism here, too?
Even the smallest spark of inspiration may have a massive impact on our results.
Don't worry. Boiling water can also be very inspiring.
Everything in the world is born of laws and regulations. There are no coincidences ...
These results are exactly as I predicted.
Stop arguing! Let's take turns ... Never mind, I'll calculate mine first.
How about a vote? ... 5 against 4. Looks like I win.
Let me think ... Non, not the way you guys think—real thinking.
Who took my pen? Number Six? Number Seven? ... Why are you all so quiet?
Time to verify our results. Any objections? Non? Bien.
This is driving me nuts! Can I just rip it to shreds?
Dosage? I don't care, just use the full dose!
Complaint letters? Hah, let them write whatever the hell they want.
What an interesting result ... It's more extreme than I'd predicted.
Aha! A little more, a little more!
Commencing decryption ... Decryption complete. That was easier than expected.
Life constantly shifts and changes—and so do I.
In theory, this hypothesis should be true.
I've already prepared a 46-page proposal for improvements.
Good, all of the collected data supports our results.
Double-Blind Experiment

To prevent your own biases from interfering, you conducted a double-blind experiment. In the end, not only did the researchers not know which group was which, but even the samples themselves seemed unaware. Nevertheless, the results still ended up falling within your expectations. Statisticians call this the "experimenter effect." Older researchers call it "getting what you wish for."
Experimental Process

An expert on methodology visited and fainted after seeing your experimental process. After regaining consciousness, he said, "You use astrology to decide when to conduct each experiment, a crystal ball to judge when it is done, and you still think you can write a paper on it?" You replied, "Hey, we did every step three times."
Soul-Searching Question

The Committee for Ethics had a question about your work: "Did your test subjects consent to that 'intangible stimulus' you use in your experiments?" You replied, "We read the consent form aloud to every petri dish." The committee members were quiet for a long time.
Inspiration at 3 AM

One researcher had a brilliant idea while showering. Still covered in soap, he rushed out to write it down. The next day, you see that he's placed a bottle of body wash on his desk, labeled "for inspiration."
Academic Debate

Two researchers argued late into the night in the lab about a small detail in a theory. Their voices got louder and louder until they had written enough formulas to cover three whole chalkboards. The next day, you spot a small note in the corner. "What were we fighting about, anyway?" Neither of them can remember, but the formulas are still there and seem somewhat useful.
Pocket Note

A researcher found a crumpled note in his pocket with parameters written in unfamiliar handwriting. He followed them, and the experiment succeeded. No one knew when that note got there or who wrote it. He pinned it up on the whiteboard. Next to it he wrote, "From: Unknown. Advice: Believe."
Blank Pages in the Logbook

When you looked through the lab log, you found a few pages in the middle that were totally blank. The page numbers came one after another, but there was nothing on them. No one remembered those pages. You wrote on the blank part: "What is on this page may be written in another dimension, or on another machine, or in the life of another group of researchers."

You held a brainstorming session. For the first half hour, people had many ideas. For the second half hour, they started telling bad jokes. For the last hour, it devolved into a serious debate: "If an idea were a gas, how heavy would one mole of it be?" You ended up with a half-decent idea and three new words that no one understood.
Mysterious Notes

You used one notebook to record all your ideas and experimental data for three years. One day, you turned to the last page. There was a line of writing that was not yours. "Read it all. Nothing interesting." You looked through the whole notebook, but you could not find which page the words were for.
Verification Obsession

A researcher would not stop until he had "checked every assumption." To do that, he made a whole set of verification tests. These verification tests were based on assumptions too, so he made tests to check the verification tests. Two weeks later, he drew a recursive diagram on the whiteboard. Next to it he wrote, "Maybe for some things, it is enough just to believe."
Boundary Value Testing

You tried to split a plan into two separate parts. You gave one part to each of two people to work on at the same time. Two weeks later, each part worked perfectly on its own. But when you put them together, they interfered with each other in a way you never could have predicted. This produced an unexpected function, which you also never could have predicted. In your report you wrote, "What people make together can sometimes go beyond what anyone planned."
Emotional Value of the Plan

A plan that everyone knew would not work was talked about seriously by the whole group for two hours. Afterward, someone asked you why you wasted all that time. You responded, "Because everyone needed to talk about a plan that was 'at least not the one we have now.'" People said it was the best meeting in a long time.

You wrote a long list of hypotheticals at the start of a plan. After each hypothetical, you wrote, "Hopefully" in parentheses. A colleague said you were being too pessimistic. You changed the notes to say, "Based on current knowledge." Another colleague said you were being too optimistic. In the end you wrote, "Tentative assumption." Everyone found that acceptable.
Missing Component

A key lab component went missing. After days of searching, it was found supporting a table leg in a researcher's home. He indignantly justified his actions: "It's still serving its purpose of 'stabilizing a structure,' isn't it?"
Mysterious Letter

You received a mysterious letter filled with harsh words and messy reasoning, yet its final suggestion greatly improved your plan. You chose not to identify the sender, but you decided to include them in the acknowledgments.

Ahem. The great Miss Matilda has arrived at her Foundation.
First, go through the security check, then walk across the main hall, and take the stairs on the left ...
Walk slower, stand straighter—I must demonstrate the true grace of the Bouanich family!
Oufph, someone just bumped into me. How rude!
Never mind, I will let it go. Ever since that recent staff expansion passed, everyone in the Foundation has been rushing around nonstop.
Next, go to the office to get the mission briefing. I should knock softly, keep smiling, and accept the documents with both hands.
Wait ... the Security Assistance Team?! Are they really assigning the protection of our alma mater to me? That's such an important job!
"I mean ... of course, no problem! Matilda, the great investigator, will do this job perfectly!"
Now, let me read what else the documents say. A map, a guide ... and the position listed is Team Leader.
Okay, now, take a deep breath. Stay calm. Do not get too proud, Matilda. Do not let your smile get too wide!
Alright, I have made a decision. Even though the mission has not officially started, I should go back to school right now and do a sweep of the patrol route to prepare.
Nothing can go wrong. Nothing!
The canteen rules are as strict as ever. There are not many risks here, but ...
Fine, I admit I do miss the canteen’s food a little.
After all, you cannot work well on an empty stomach!
Hmph, there are so many new dishes now. Why do these things always happen after you graduate?
But if I had to pick one thing to eat, I would go for the classic meatballs with gravy.
It is ranked the most popular dish in the canteen?
What can I say? My taste is impeccable!
The handmade meatballs have just the right balance of lean and fat, fried until golden and fragrant, then covered in a rich sauce that is both savory and slightly sweet. Mmm ...
Thinking back, there was a girl who loved chocolate very much.
For two weeks, she ate nothing but plain noodles to trade all her meatballs for chocolate bars. Honestly, how extreme can someone be?
Oh, I remember, that was Merel!
Her love for sweets is quite similar to Vertin's. But at least Vertin would never let herself go hungry!
Then again, I wonder where she even gets all those toffee candies in her pocket.
And Sonetto ... She was never picky at all.
I watched her for a long time but could never figure out her favorite food.
She could even accept pineapple pizza. Well, it is nice to be open-minded, but fruit on pizza ... Yuck!
Ah, it has been a while since I have gotten to see everyone. I wonder if I will get the chance to sit in the canteen with everyone again after returning this time.
The library is one of the few places in school meant for relaxation.
Aside from the canteen, it is the most popular place for students to spend their free time.
Emergency exits, evacuation routes, opening and closing times for the ceremony day ...
Good, I have it all memorized.
The library looks like it has a lot of books, but it is just the same kinds over and over. It never seems to change.
This old book ...
Oh, this is the Fiddler Crab Shapeshifting book Merel mentioned before!
Back then, I borrowed a much thicker and more complex book on shapeshifting. It was so boring that I fell asleep many times while reading it, and I never did learn how to do it.
Hmph, that is not because the great Matilda lacks intelligence. There is simply no need to spend too much time on such niche topics!
But why did I even borrow that book in the first place?
Aha, this is the small literature section. Of course, those two troublemakers, Vertin and Merel, borrowed almost all the fun books. But a truly good student would not let herself get lost in stories!
Wait, the borrowers listed for this copy of "Mother Goose" are ... Isabella and "The Ring."
After the job is done, I will come back to the library and borrow this book.
There are five watchtowers on campus.
When I was a student, seeing them from afar always reminded me of the many-eyed giant of legend. I used to imagine a teacher standing on each tower, watching the entire school day and night.
Places that were once off-limits are now open to me.
But this staircase seems to go on forever ...
Does that mean that during my patrol, I will have to climb stairs like these five whole times? Maybe ten, or even fifteen times?!
I-I feel a little dizzy already ...
Stay strong, Matilda. The maintenance team does this as well. You can manage it!
Phew ... I finally made it to the top.
Now this "Shelter Dove User and Maintenance Guide" should prove useful. Honestly, I wanted to throw it away several times on the way up!
I do not understand. Why did the writers go through all the trouble of writing a guide, only to include such confusing instructions anyway?
First, do this, then do that ... done!
Before the official patrol begins, I should summarize the key steps and write them down for quick reference.
Then that assistant will see just how capable and professional Team Leader Matilda is!
They have already put up the fences for the opening ceremony.
This year, the school has admitted many orphaned arcanists. This whole place will probably be full of new students. Most of the guards will be here to keep things in order.
Oufph! My ears!
Alright, this volume should be more than enough to reach even the students dozing in the back.
The ceremony will follow the usual routine and last half the morning. The same choir, the same speech from the principal, the same school motto ...
Cloudy weather is the best. Too much sun can make people feel faint. If it rains, everyone has to stand with umbrellas ...
A classmate once complained that a rainy ceremony felt like attending a funeral.
Speaking of the choir, how long has it been since that ceremony?
The students who managed to "leave" the school after that never returned. Much later, Vertin told me that the only thing waiting for them outside the school gate that year was the "Storm."
After that, I had to admit that the school's very strict rules were not for no reason.

But I am no longer who I was back then. If anyone tries to cause trouble during this ceremony, I, the former monitor assistant, and now the great investigator and a proud alumna, will stop them and protect the younger students!

On this day in 1903, the first Tour de France set off from Paris. The race has since become one of the world's most famous road cycling races.
On this day in 1961, Hemingway passed away in his home. Marcus read through "The Snows of Kilimanjaro" in quiet remembrance of the great novelist.
Today, Brume visits the Carl Benz Memorial Antique Car Show, stopping to take in each exhibit at length.
To mark the anniversary of Mars Pathfinder's landing on Mars, Regulus plays David Bowie's "Life on Mars?" in the Suitcase.
In 1994, a young American launched an online bookstore from his garage. Word has it that books about arcanum found their way into the catalog as well.
While helping the Foundation sort its display room collection, Loggerhead finds that a 1962 talk show recording has gone missing—only to later find it in her satchel.
When asked whether she has read The Adventures of Pinocchio, Voyager smiles and plays "March of the Wooden Soldiers" in reply.
Lilya challenges a pilot friend to a friendly race, with Lilya on a flying broomstick and her friend in a jet.
In 1962, Andy Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans was first exhibited at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles, sparking the pop art movement.
Vila comes across Lady by the Lake on a wall and starts asking her questions about Cubism.
Inspired and encouraged by Regulus, Paper Heron has drawn up an initial plan to set sail with her mule.
Regulus invites Coppélia to a heavy metal concert. Coppélia is a little scared by the words "heavy metal," but Regulus won't take no for an answer.
The "Danube Dawn" adds a special item to its cargo list—the illustrated book Rubuska keeps going on about, Stribor's Forest.
Ms. Moissan teaches Paper Heron a unique variant of mahjong. Paper Heron picks it up quickly.
On the anniversary of the Gamicom's release, J brings one into the Suitcase and spends the whole day playing Popeye.
After finishing her exorcism work for the night, Ramona listens to a ranchera song called "Camino de la Montaña" on her way home.
On this day in history, Handel performed Water Music for the first time at a concert held on a barge.
A certain computer manufacturer once invited the director of Laplace to attend their event, but the director ultimately declined due to being likely to trigger their security protocols.
In 1912, a meteorite exploded over Holbrook, Arizona, showering the area with stones. Laplace analyzed its composition and confirmed that no arcane energy was present.
When Moldir was young, she once fell from a horse and was rescued by Ivan. She promised to wash his beloved horse for a week so he wouldn't tell her father what really happened.

In a study on the history of railway development, Corvus learns about the opening of the Trans-Siberian Railway. She can't help imagining how she would coordinate and manage the longest railway line in the world.
In 1933, American pilot Wiley Post completed the first solo circumnavigation of the globe by airplane.

In 1962, an artificial satellite relayed the first transatlantic television broadcast signal. Some of the first images to cross the ocean included the Statue of Liberty in New York and the Eiffel Tower in Paris.
Liang Yue invites Paper Heron to try the mapo tofu at a Chinese restaurant. To her disappointment, Paper Heron has nothing to say about the taste and only praises its appearance.
In 1909, a monoplane achieved the first airplane flight across the English Channel. Flutterpage is very curious about how a monoplane gets off the ground.
After noting that "Coppélia knows little about Alice in Wonderland," Loggerhead sits down with her in the Suitcase to watch Alice's story from beginning to end.
In 1921, insulin was isolated from a dog's pancreas for the first time, offering a way to eliminate the fatal symptoms of diabetes.
It is an especially hot, dry midsummer. Along the Don, farmers and horses laze in the shallows, staring blankly at the fields. The wounds of war have already been swallowed by golden waves of wheat.
In 1836, the Arc de Triomphe in Paris was inaugurated. It has since become a national symbol of France.
Strolling through Paris, Sentinel can't take her eyes off what the passersby are wearing. In a letter to a close friend, she wonders whether her taste can still keep up with the latest fashions.
In 1954, an Italian expedition became the first to summit K2, the second-highest mountain on Earth.

Welcome to the Future

Welcome to Facility 3826, Comrade!
Have you witnessed the latest innovations in Soviet robotics? These modern marvels aren't just limited to factory work; they will aid humans as servants and companions in every aspect of our lives! We have the VOV-A6 Lab Tech, the RAF-9 Engineer, the MUC-1 Drofa, the WSP-9 Pchela ... You can find them all here in Facility 3826! We can't wait to introduce our robotic assistants to you and the whole world!

You may have seen similar devices here in Chelomey before. These Multiblockers are an important part of our security system. Each of them is a micro robot that can lock its own door when necessary and can only be unlocked via human instruction.
They are usually installed in classified areas to safeguard critical assets.

Reply: The Radio of the Future is playing "Our Guiding Star." All we can hear is the engines roaring The gentlemen are drunk and puffing smoke The ladies are wearing furs of extinct animals Who can tell what the future will be like? All we can hear is the engines roaring Away from the Earth, we are led by a guiding star

Breaking news! A major breakthrough in scientific education: introducing Neuro-Polymer!
Backed by Dr. Sechenov's comprehensive educational program, this technology allows users to instantly acquire professional knowledge in any field, saving decades of study! After a single injection, you will be able to speak any language or play any instrument ... From now on, barriers to knowledge will be no more! This astounding new technology is a gift to all of humanity, one that we look forward to sharing with the whole world!

Never stop dreaming, as through collective action we will make all our dreams come true! Thanks to the brilliance of Neuro-Polymer and the process of mimetic adaptation, we are only one step away from starting the greatest technological revolution in human history!
Soon robots will take over the mundane operation of our society, freeing humanity from the back-breaking labor that has kept us in chains for thousands of years! Join us now, Comrade, and embrace a limitless future!
